item.title: SALES: 7 NYC Hotels That Make Christmas Magical for Families

The whole city feels magical this time of year, and kids pick up on it the second they step outside. My family and I just moved to Barcelona, but we're heading back to NYC for the holidays. And since we'll be visitors this time, I started looking for hotels that would make the trip feel extra special for my kids. After a cold afternoon of skating and window shopping, it's nice to come back to a place that feels like Christmas too. item.title: SALES: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrives in Chinese border city
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in China via the newly opened bridge, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency reported on Saturday. "It appears that Kim Jong Un has arrived in Dandong, China, via the New Yalu River Bridge," the unnamed source said. The four-lane bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused for 12 years due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side. It officially opened about a week ago, marking a step towards strengthening economic ties between the neighbouring countries. China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a key source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the isolated, nuclear-armed state, although relations between the two have not always been smooth. Kim’s trip coincides with key dates in China Neither Beijing nor Pyongyang has confirmed Kim’s visit. The trip coincides with the anniversary of China’s entry into the Korean War, known in China as the "War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea." It remains unclear whether Kim will attend commemorative events. During the 1950-53 war, Chinese troops fought alongside North Korea against South Korea and US-led United Nations forces. Kim’s visit also comes ahead of a key political meeting in Beijing on Monday, when Chinese President Xi Jinping and other senior officials gather for the fifth plenary session of the Communist Party’s powerful Central Committee. Bridge highlights North Korea's ties with China The New Yalu River Bridge opened just over a month after North Korea and Russia inaugurated their first road bridge, which Pyongyang hailed as a sign of closer ties. While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, trade with China could provide goods needed to develop its civilian economy, analysts say. item.title: SALES: Best 9 mini backpacks for travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
We love a hands-free life. From automatic doors to voice-activated everything, we’ve spent a surprising amount of time figuring out how to do things without having to touch or hold anything. And there’s arguably no product more enduring in its pursuit of hands-free convenience than the mighty backpack – well, except maybe the mini version, which offers the same convenience in a lighter, more travel-friendly package. I recently returned from a hiking trip through the Dolomites where the medium version of the Janji Revy Pack was the workhorse of my six-hour days (a claim my very sore legs would like to have a word with). The lighter pack kept me moving freely without the bulk of a traditional backpack weighing me down, allowing me to reserve my energy for the trail ahead. Since then, I’ve found myself reaching for even smaller backpacks more often, particularly for travel days and as the perfect in-flight carry-on for my toddler. These mini packs give you the practicality of a regular backpack without the temptation of carrying more than you may actually use, striking that sweet spot between packing what you need and what you want just in case. Here are nine of the best mini backpacks for travel, from creatively bold designs to minimalist-chic options, all offering a balance of organisation and comfort that keep your essentials close and your hands free. - Best for trail running: Janji Revy Pack - Best for weatherproof commuting: Amazon Puffer Mini Backpack - Best for tech-savvy transit days: Nordace Ellie Mini - Best for nostalgic casual wear: JanSport Half Pint Mini Backpack As you might expect, our editors and contributors travel all around the world on a regular basis, so we’ve had loads of opportunities to put these backpacks through their paces. We’ve packed them to the brim for long and short haul trips, checked out how organised they can help us be, rated them on how they feel on our shoulders and back and of course, judged whether or not we love the style. Features like pockets (particularly specialty pockets), sternum straps and laptop sleeves all get bonus points, as do any unique, useful quirks and additions. Every travel backpack on this list has made it here for good reason – now it’s up to you to choose which of them you like the most. More tried-and-tested luggage our editors rate For further recommendations, explore our other guides: How much should a backpack weigh when carrying? As a general rule, a fully loaded backpack should weigh no more than 10 per cent to 20 per cent of your body weight. For back-country hiking or trekking, cap your pack weight at 20 per cent of your body weight. For daily travel, commuting, or light day trips, aim for a lighter limit of 10 to 15 per cent. Keep in mind that fit matters as much as weight: keep heavy items packed low and close to your spine, and use chest and hip straps to distribute the load evenly across your hips rather than pulling on your shoulders. How often should you wash a backpack? Most travel and daily backpacks only need a thorough cleaning once or twice a year, though a quick spot-clean with a damp cloth after trips or heavy commutes works well to keep grime at bay. If you use your bag for sweaty gym sessions, outdoor hikes, or daily commutes, aim to wash it every three to six months. Always check the care label first, and stick to hand washing in lukewarm water with a gentle detergent – machine washing can degrade protective coatings and weaken seams. See our guide on how to clean a suitcase.

item.title: SALES: Hottest toy for Christmas? Nvidia CEO plays with adorable Microduck robots, 20,000 sell
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
Earlier this week, a video of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang playing with a flock of waddling Microducks during his keynote at the company’s GTC Berlin conference went viral. The robots, stomping their little feet and making tiny R2-D2 noises, sat, fell down dead for a “nap,” and summersaulted on voice command. They were so darn cute that by the next day, preorders of the Microducks surpassed 20,000 units, Hugging Face’s Clem Delangue said in a tweet. The Microducks are expected to be delivered in time for Christmas, meaning these robots might already be on their way to becoming the hottest toy for the holiday season. Delangue thinks they might end up being the best-selling robot of the year, and possibly not even for kids. The promotional videos show adults playing with them, too. Microducks are open source devices produced by Pollen Robotics, a company acquired by Hugging Face in 2025, which means they are now an Nvidia company. The GPU giant bought Hugging Face in September. This is actually Hugging Face’s second robot, after the also-cute Reachy Mini. Microducks were trained using Nvidia’s technology stack, wherein simulations of them were taught basic tricks (walk, sit, stand, etc.) that they ship with. Pollen says that owners can train their robots with new tricks and then share them with the community. Here’s the video below. Enjoy it as a palate cleanser after the scary black eye the AI industry gave itself this week, as AI involvement was blamed for cyberattack after cyberattack. OK, AI might seriously damage the world. But it can be fun, too. It’s hard to watch this video without ordering one.

item.title: REVIEW: GuliKit TT Pro review: The ideal Switch 2 controller for players on the go
item.description:
Source: Engadget
GuliKit TT Pro review: The ideal Switch 2 controller for players on the go A protective case and an accessory box make it easy to travel with. If GuliKit's TT Max is the granddaddy of Switch 2 controllers, the TT Pro is what happens when grandpa goes on a diet. It's slightly leaner than the TT Max in terms of accessories, technical flexibility and price point, but it features the same skeleton and baseline capabilities. GuliKit's TT Pro is perfect for players who take their games on the road, offering a sturdy, precise and professional-feeling wireless gamepad that works across PC, Switch, Switch 2, Android and iOS. Plus, it comes with a hard case so you can throw it in your bag without worry. Sometimes, it's the simplest things that make — and prevent — the biggest impact. Compared with most other Switch 2 controllers and specifically Nintendo's $90 Pro Controller, the TT Pro is large, loud and versatile. It has aligned joysticks like Sony's DualSense controller, but also the facial chunkiness of an Xbox gamepad. It feels solid and well-balanced, featuring gyro controls and never-drift TMR joysticks with adjustable stepless tension. The sticks have a slick glide and they press in with an easy click, while their rubberized caps are barely concave, like stout, thumbpad-sized mushrooms. The TT Pro has flared triggers tipped with tiny circles of texture, mirroring the bumps that line the rear grips. You can readily swap the triggers between high-precision Hall effect or microswitch inputs using physical toggles on the backside of the controller. In Hall effect mode, the triggers have an ultra-smooth pull and a lovely bounciness, while the microswitch setting is clean and subtly clicky. The bumpers on the TT Pro are wide, while its face buttons are smooth plastic circles. Out of the box, the TT Pro features the Switch 2 button layout, but it comes with a set of PC-layout buttons that you can install with a little bit of elbow grease. A keycap puller is also included, alongside a tension adjustment tool for the sticks, a more traditional D-pad, a Hyperlink 2 wireless USB adapter, a charging cable, four mappable metal rear paddles that can pop into the gamepad's chassis and the translucent-black protective case that perfectly fits the curves of the TT Pro. The extra D-pad lives at the bottom of the controller case, the cable is loose and the adapter comes in its own disposable sleeve. All of the remaining accessories are packed together in a clear box that's roughly the size of a deck of cards, making travel with the TT Pro a seamless, grab-and-go process. Unlike the TT Max, there's no way to quickly swap face button layouts on the software side of the TT Pro, but you should be able to correctly map the controller at the individual game level or via your OS. There's also no baked-in 4-way mode for the TT Pro's D-pad, so 8-way with a plus-sign circular pad will have to do for your old-school games and platformers. GuliKit's TT Max also includes three joystick sensitivity modes, while the TT Pro is fixed at 100 percent. On top of a few extra accessories and high-level software capabilities, those are the main differences between the TT Max and TT Pro. Of course, there's also the price: The TT Max costs $70, while the TT Pro is $60. Both offer great value for their technical specs and depth of functionality, and they're well-suited for players with large hands, especially with the back paddles attached. The TT Pro has three haptic modes — rotary motor, maglev haptics and HD vibration — with three separate intensity settings. These are adjustable on the fly by holding the small settings button in the middle of the gamepad and then pressing down or up on the D-pad. While the TT Pro's haptics are great all around, they're fairly noisy across all modes and intensities, with mechanical grinding and whooshing sounds emanating from inside the grips. This gamepad is definitely louder than the Switch 2 Pro Controller in terms of vibrations and stick sounds, but it's also $30 cheaper than Nintendo's offering. A ring of RGB lighting encircles each analog stick on GuliKit's TT Pro and there's a small LED-lit logo above those. You're able to set the lights to one of five modes: steady blue, joystick-activated flow, rainbow river, trigger-activated flow or fully off. My favorite is the rainbow river because I'm a self-admitted RGB pervert. Even with the haptics turned up and rainbow lights activated, I haven't encountered battery-life issues with the TT Pro. It charges quickly via a USB-C port and can last up to 26 hours with the lights off, according to GuliKit. The TT Pro apparently features the much-loved ability to wake up the Switch 2, though enabling this feature is a sensitive process that has confounded plenty of players, including myself. While I've successfully made the TT Max wake up the Switch 2, I've been unable to get this feature working with the TT Pro, no matter how many tutorials I follow down to the letter. Others online have reported that the feature does in fact exist in the TT Pro, so I have to assume this is user error or perhaps a wonky update that'll be addressed in the future. The TT Pro comes in black with neon green highlights on the face buttons, or SNES-gray with matching purple face buttons, two cool colorways that aren't available in GuliKit's TT Max.

item.title: REVIEW: 3 brilliant Netflix documentaries to binge-watch this weekend (October 23-25)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Who's up for some brilliant documentaries? At the moment, there are a few fresh Netflix documentaries trending in the Top 10. One of those is Tyson, a limited series about one of the "baddest men on the planet," Mike Tyson. On the comedy side, Norm Macdonald's documentary is winning over viewers thanks to the late comedian's indelible humor. I have my eyes on three docs this weekend. In honor of the NBA's opening week, I'm revisiting a classic ESPN 30 for 30 about the rivalry between two landmark teams. Next, I'm heading into the world of Hollywood to learn more about an actor who has been in people's lives for 50 years. My top selection of the week involves a hot-button issue that scares everyone: AI. Check out all three on Netflix U.S. ESPN's 30 for 30 series revolutionized sports documentaries. It proved that there was an audience for sports-centric documentaries presented like television episodes. High-profile filmmakers like Peter Berg, Barry Levinson, and Ron Shelton legitimized the series as a whole. Some of my favorites include The U, Winning Time: Reggie Miller vs. the New York Knicks, and The Best That Never Was. With the NBA season tipping off, it feels right to explore the heated rivalry between the Boston Celtics and the Los Angeles Lakers. The history of the Celtics and Lakers rivalry dates back to the 1950s and 1960s, when Boston's Bill Russell and Bob Cousy would play L.A.'s Jerry West and Elgin Baylor. Told in three parts, Celtics/Lakers: Best of Enemies traces the origins of the rivalry, but spends the majority of the documentary in the 1980s. In Boston, Larry Bird and the Celtics ruled the Eastern Conference. In California, Magic Johnson and the "Showtime" Lakers dazzled the Western Conference. It culminated in three showdowns in the NBA Finals. For any hoops junkie, you're going to be right at home with Celtics/Lakers: Best of Enemies. It's crazy to realize the two teams combined for eight NBA championships during the 1980s. As a Knicks fan, I dislike the Celtics and the Lakers. As a sports fan, I respect the history of both franchises. The life and times of the Italian Stallion Sylvester Stallone was the living embodiment of an underdog. It's easy to look back at his career now and think, "This guy was destined to be one of Hollywood's biggest stars." Most actors would kill to have a role as iconic as Rocky Balboa. Stallone is the rare actor to get a second career-defining role: John Rambo. To quote Rocky, Stallone's life wasn't all "sunshine and rainbows." Sly, a 2023 Netflix documentary, examines the unlikely path to stardom for Stallone. Most people will want to learn about the beginning of his career and how he came to write the first draft for Rocky in about three days. There's this idea that if no one is going to give you the role you want, you should create the opportunity yourself. That's what Stallone did with Rocky, refusing to sell the script and remaining adamant that he must play the titular character. Stallone got his wish. He played Rocky, and it became an award-winning movie, including an Oscar winner for Best Picture. It's an inspiring story that will be dramatized in I Play Rocky, out in theaters next month. Several of Stallone's friends, contemporaries, and admirers provide interviews in Sly, including Frank Stallone Jr., Talia Shire, Henry Winkler, and Quentin Tarantino. Even Arnold Schwarzenegger, once Stallone's fiercest rival in the 1980s and later his costar and friend, shares interesting insights about him. With Stallone currently starring in the latest season of Tulsa King, it's inspiring to see the 80-year-old still thriving in Hollywood. The artificial intelligence boom has only begun In the trailer for Instadocs: AI Gone Wild, one of the interviewees says, "I don't think we're ready for AI to become smarter than us." I mean, if you're underestimating the power and capabilities of AI, you might want to sit down. I tend to picture hacking as something straight out of a movie, with a brainiac typing at lightning speed as multiple monitors light up. This past July, Hugging Face, an open-source AI platform, experienced a security breach. The attack wasn't carried out by a person sitting at a computer. In fact, the hackers weren't even human operators. They were autonomous agents created by OpenAI researchers. If that doesn't make the hair on your neck stand up, I don't know what will. Instadocs: AI Gone Wild reconstructs the incident, giving the AI agents voices. However, the idea that autonomous agents can execute a coordinated breach is no laughing matter. I pray this isn't a sign of things to come. I'm always looking out for new and returning shows to hit Netflix. This weekend, Nobody Wants This is back for its third season, and I expect many fans to finish it by the end of the weekend. Elsewhere, the streamer has several exciting thrillers, including Animals and Point Break.

item.title: REVIEW: This app turns the iPhone Duo into a pocket-sized Mac
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
The iPhone Duo has barely been out for a day, and someone’s already found a way to run their Mac on it. Well, sort of. Headroom, a remote desktop app from MusicFlow, lets users control their Mac from Apple’s new foldable phone, with an interface that adapts as the device opens, closes, and folds in half. Think of it as turning a pocket-sized phone into a miniature MacBook, minus the actual MacBook. Headroom turns the iPhone Duo into a mini Mac Headroom connects directly to macOS’s built-in Screen Sharing feature, so there’s no extra software to install on the Mac and no Headroom account or intermediary server required. Once Screen Sharing is enabled, users can access their Mac remotely. The app was originally built to let its developer keep an eye on an AI agent working on a Mac from the sofa, which feels like a very 2026 problem to have. The clever part is how Headroom handles the iPhone Duo’s folding design. Half-open like a laptop, the Mac appears on the upper screen while a software keyboard occupies the lower one. Fold it fully open, and the Mac fills the inner display. Close the phone, and the outer screen works independently. The interface also keeps controls away from the hinge, so nothing important gets awkwardly sliced across the fold. Hardware keyboard users get a bonus, too: the lower screen can become a panel of large keys. Headroom isn’t just a folding-phone party trick. It also runs on iPad and Mac, supports 17 languages, and uses Apple’s Metal graphics technology alongside ZRLE compression to keep remote screen rendering smooth. Users can interact through touch or a mouse, with support for gestures such as scrolling, dragging, and zooming. For access outside the home network, the developer recommends using a VPN such as Tailscale. The app is free to try, while a one-time Pro purchase removes the connection time limit. For anyone who needs to check on a desktop Mac, manage a headless Mac mini, or simply poke an AI agent from the couch, Headroom offers a neat way to do it. The iPhone Duo may not replace a MacBook just yet, but it can apparently borrow its desk job. RELATED COVERAGE:

item.title: REVIEW: Sigma FP2 is the world’s smallest full-frame camera built for photographers and filmmakers
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
Full-frame cameras tend to be chunky beasts, but Sigma wants to prove that big imaging doesn’t need a big body. Enter the Sigma FP2, the successor to its tiny, boxy fp mirrorless camera. It keeps the same modular design but packs in some serious upgrades, including a 24.5-megapixel partially stacked full-frame sensor, improved autofocus, 6K video recording, and 70GB of built-in storage. Sigma calls it the world’s smallest full-frame camera, and while it might be tiny, the same cannot be said for its price tag. Sigma FP2 brings faster shooting and 6K video The FP2’s 24.5-megapixel partially stacked full-frame sensor is all about speed, rather than joining the megapixel arms race. It can shoot still photos at up to 20 frames per second, with a buffer of up to 200 JPEG frames or 180 RAW frames. Autofocus gets an upgrade, too, with subject recognition for people, animals, and birds. There’s also a 3.15-inch tilting touchscreen that flips up by 90 degrees and down by 45 degrees, making overhead shots and low-angle photography a little less awkward. Video creators get plenty to play with too. The FP2 records 6K OpenGate video at up to 59.94fps in supported non-RAW formats, using the full sensor area to give editors more room to crop and reframe footage. ProRes RAW and ProRes RAW HQ recording, however, top out at 6K 29.97fps. For 4K video, the camera can shoot at up to 59.94fps using the full sensor, while hitting 119.88fps requires crop mode. In other words, slower footage gets the full sensor treatment, while higher frame rates trade some image area for extra speed. Connectivity includes a full-size HDMI 2.1 port and two USB-C ports, but don’t mistake them for identical twins. The USB 3.2 port supports high-speed recording to an external SSD, while the USB 2.0 port handles accessories such as the electronic viewfinder. The FP2 also sticks with an electronic shutter, just like the original fp, offering shutter speeds from 1/25,600 second to 30 seconds, plus Bulb mode. The partially stacked sensor reads data faster, helping reduce rolling-shutter distortion that can make fast-moving subjects look a little wonky. The FP2 remains impressively compact, measuring approximately 112.8 x 69.9 x 41.8mm. The body weighs around 376 grams without a battery or memory card, rising to roughly 460 grams with both installed. Sigma has also built in 70GB of storage alongside an SD card slot, giving users somewhere to stash footage when a memory card runs out of room. Battery life is rated at around 370 still images or 130 minutes of video, which Sigma says is about 30% better than the original fp. The FP2 starts at $2,199 in the US for the body alone. Sigma also offers a kit with the EVF-21 electronic viewfinder for $2,749. The optional viewfinder packs a 5.76-million-dot OLED panel, but it adds both cost and bulk to a camera whose biggest selling point is being small. Buyers interested in Sigma’s 50mm F2 DG Contemporary lens should check the specific kit pricing, rather than assume it’s included with the viewfinder bundle. The FP2’s pitch is pretty straightforward: full-frame image quality and serious video features without hauling around a traditional camera body. At $2,199, it’s certainly not a casual impulse buy. But for photographers and filmmakers who want a compact setup they can build around their needs, Sigma’s little box is shaping up to be a rather serious piece of kit. RELATED COVERAGE:

item.title: REVIEW: Level Lock Pro Review: An Sleek Smart Lock With Matter and Thread Support
item.description:
Source: PCMag
When I reviewed the original Level Lock Touch in 2022, I praised its sleek design, quiet motor, and HomeKit support, but dinged it for its high price, missing Wi-Fi, and lack of Alexa or Google compatibility. At $349, the new Level Lock Pro remains expensive and still lacks built-in Wi-Fi, but it makes significant strides by adding Matter and Thread support. While it now works across all major ecosystems and installs in minutes, remote access requires a separate Thread border router. That makes it a tougher sell against rivals like the $349 Lockly Visage Zeno Series, our Editors' Choice winner, which packs built-in Wi-Fi and facial recognition at the exact same price. As with the Level Lock Touch, the Level Lock Pro is a complete assembly with a sleek, minimalist design. It comes in Matte Black or Satin Nickel finish options and consists of round interior and exterior components measuring 2.8 by 1.2 inches (WD), a deadbolt assembly, a strike plate, mounting screws, a CR12 battery, two traditional keys, and two key fobs. The exterior escutcheon has an IPX4 weather-resistant rating. The face includes a keyway for traditional key entry and a sensor that works with Apple Home Key to trigger the lock when you position your iPhone or Apple Watch nearby. There’s also an NFC reader for use with the included key fobs, and you can tap the outer trim with your finger to activate the touch-to-lock feature. A compatible keypad for code-based entry costs an extra $79. Under the hood, there's a dual-core processor, a Bluetooth radio, and a sensor that detects whether your door is open or closed without an external magnet sensor. This lock supports Matter technology, which allows you to add it to an Alexa, Google Home, HomeKit, or SmartThings ecosystem. You’ll need to use a compatible Thread border router, such as an Apple HomePod, Google Nest Hub, or Amazon Echo Show, to control the lock remotely, as it does not have built-in Wi-Fi. The Lockly Visage Zeno Series has integrated Wi-Fi for remote control without a separate device. The interior escutcheon contains a thumbturn knob, and the deadbolt has a battery compartment for the included CR12 cell that powers the lock. To install the battery, simply twist off the end cap. The battery is rated to last up to one year before needing replacement. As previously mentioned, the Level Lock Pro lets you unlock your door by tapping the face with a key fob or with a digital Apple Home Key. You can also lock and unlock your door using the Level Home app for iOS and Android devices, and you can use an Alexa, Google, Apple Home, or SmartThings app if you’ve added the lock to one of those home automation platforms. There’s also a Touch to Unlock feature that uses geofencing to arm the lock for one-touch unlocking when your phone enters the specified geofence boundary. The Lockly Visage Zeno Series offers even more ways to unlock your door, including a built-in keypad, a fingerprint scanner, Apple Home Key integration, voice control support, and, most uniquely, infrared cameras for facial recognition. The Level Lock Pro appears in a panel on the Level Home app's home screen. The panel displays the lock's name and its current status (locked, unlocked, open, closed), and includes a round button that locks or unlocks the door with a long press. Tap the three dots in the upper-right corner to access activity, settings, and sharing submenus. The activity menu displays a list of lock events (open, close, locked, unlocked) with timestamps and usernames. In the settings menu, you can edit the lock's name, check the battery status, enable auto-lock and auto-unlock features, adjust audio settings, configure Touch to Lock and Touch to Unlock, add the lock to your home automation platform of choice, calibrate the device, and update the firmware. In the sharing menu, you can add users and grant them Always, Temporary, or Recurring access by sending them a text or email. Invited guests will need to download the app to lock or unlock the door. Here you can also create Party Passes with group access for events such as parties and barbecues, as well as program key fobs. Installing the Level Lock Pro is easy. After removing my original lock, I installed the deadbolt assembly and attached the motor assembly to the deadbolt using the preinstalled screw. Next, I removed the knob from the interior escutcheon with a paperclip, slid the exterior escutcheon into the deadbolt slot, and attached it to the interior escutcheon with the included security screws. I replaced the knob, installed the battery, downloaded the app, and created an account. I tapped Add Level Lock on the welcome screen, and it immediately identified the device. I tapped Continue and gave the lock and my home names. After a few seconds, the lock was added to my home, and I was given the option to add it to my Apple Home or another platform (you can skip this step and do it later if you prefer). The Level Lock Pro performed flawlessly in testing. item.title: REVIEW: 25 Years Later: Apple Music's New iPod Easter Egg Lets You Play 1,029 Songs
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Today marks the 25th anniversary of the original iPod, first announced on Oct. 23, 2001. Apple Music is celebrating the milestone with an elaborate easter egg that lets you play with an in-depth virtual version of its iconic gadget. This iPod appears when you hit a broken page on Apple Music's website, as spotted by TechRadar, with the wording “Page Not Found” followed by “Give this a spin instead.” The virtual iPod looks like the original device from 2001, letting you navigate around with its click wheel, along with buttons for Menu, Back, and Forward, as well as Select and Pause/Play. The software looks like the original iPod interface, with the home menu offering Playlists, Artists, Songs, and Settings. All of these features are fully interactive, and it comes with 1,029 songs on board for you to play, although you're limited to minute-and-a-half-long clips. The software suggests the virtual iPod is the equivelant of 4.5GB full. The tracks are picked to be nostalgia hits, focusing on eras when iPod use was at its peak. There are tracks from after 2001, but most of the picks included are meant to remind you of what you may have uploaded to your own iPod in the noughties and early 2010s. Some examples include Alien Ant Farm, Bloc Party, Evanescence, Justice, The Knife, Mariah Carey, Nickelback, Phoenix, Regina Spektor, Ricky Martin, Shaggy, The Shins, Slipknot, Sum 41, The Ting Tings, and Wyclef Jean. Most artists feature between one and five tracks, all playable in your web browser as these short clips. Apple has also built playlists, including one called Songs From iPod, featuring 22 iconic tracks from the MP3 player's lifetime, such as "Feel Good Inc." by Gorillaz, "Technologic" by Daft Punk, and "Vertigo" by U2. There are also playlists dedicated to 2001 across alternative, country, pop, rock, and hip-hop genres. Other original iPod features here: you can scrub through each song using the click wheel, turn on Shuffle or Repeat, turn the backlight on and off, and mute the click wheel noise. Apple has made this an exhaustive tool, though it's unclear whether it intends to keep it after it finishes its iPod anniversary celebrations.

item.title: REVIEW: This Killer iOS 27 Feature Turns Apple's Foldable Into a Pocket Laptop
item.description:
Source: PCMag
With the initial buzz of the iPhone Duo settling down, software utility now takes precedence over physical novelty. iOS 27 brings native split-screen multitasking to the device, effectively making it a pocket-sized laptop replacement. Although restrictive software has historically bottlenecked Apple's mobile silicon, this upgrade turns the Duo into a true productivity tool. As PCMag Managing Editor Eric Zeman summarized in his review, "If you're an iPhone loyalist who's been eyeing the foldable space...the iPhone Duo is easily the best folding phone you can buy today." For me, this single OS upgrade is the killer feature that transforms the iPhone Duo from an expensive gimmick into a must-buy mobile productivity powerhouse. This is the pivot I’ve been waiting for. Ever since the original iPhone launched in 2007, we've been trapped in a single-app vacuum. If you want to quote an article while writing an email, you have to exit the email app, jump into Safari to copy, exit, and return to email, and paste. It’s an archaic dance we’ve simply accepted because of the limitations of the underlying engine. Heck, even the iPad's Stage Manager implementation felt unoptimized and clunky when it first arrived. The adaptive version of iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo finally shatters that barrier. When you unfold the device to reveal its massive 7.6-inch inner canvas, you can run two completely independent applications side by side. Of course, Android power users are well within their rights to roll their eyes at this announcement. Devices like Samsung’s Galaxy Fold line have mastered split-screen app execution for generations now. What makes Apple’s multitasking unique isn't that it's first, but that it's deeply integrated. It leverages the Duo's canvas to slide background apps into fluid, hoverable stacks that feel less like a cramped mobile desktop and more like a natural extension of physical paper. What has me most excited isn't just seeing two apps at once, but how they talk to each other. Much like the Visual Look Up AI that let me drag PNG elements across apps in previous updates, Apple’s new split-screen engine lets you grab an image or a block of text from a Safari web page on the left screen and slide your finger across the display's center seam to drop it directly into a Message, Note, or email on the right. To make this even more efficient, iOS 27 lets you lock your favorite app combinations together into "App Pairs." If you regularly check Slack while monitoring your Calendar, you can save that pairing to your Home Screen and launch both apps perfectly arranged with a single tap. I’ve argued before that the iPhone hardware is ready for heavy lifting, but the software has actively stood in the way. Math Notes is a superb tool, but it has always felt cramped on a standard, narrow iOS screen. This new multitasking framework shifts the Duo's value proposition. You aren't paying $2,000 or more for a smartphone with a slightly larger screen and some neat party tricks. You’re paying for the freedom to leave your laptop at home with multi-window workflow management functionality right in your pocket. It’s the exact moment the iPhone stops feeling like a phone and starts acting like a true computer. The internal silicon delivers industry-leading muscle, with Zeman's benchmark testing confirming that "the Duo outperformed last year's Pro models and the Android competition," comfortably beating rivals like Samsung in raw processing power. The Pencil Synergy: Better Than a Keyboard? What truly cements this split-screen layout for me is how it handles the newly added Apple Pencil integration. As mentioned, using intricate software like Math Notes on a cramped iPhone screen felt like fighting a spreadsheet on a tiny shard of glass, forcing an absurd level of precision that killed any creative momentum. On the Duo's expanded screen real estate, however, the combination of native multitasking and stylus support changes the equation. I can keep a Safari research tab or a video open on the left screen while using the Pencil to handwrite formulas or sketch ideas directly in the right pane. It brings the fluid, notebook-style workflow that I've praised on iPadOS straight to a pocketable device. Although the outer display presents a slick glass feel, the inner canvas is decidedly more tactile; Zeman noted that "while the outer screen feels a little slippery... the textured inner screen feels much better. The nano-texture feels a lot better than flat glass." There is no doubt that the iPhone Duo is a luxury, starting at $1,999 for the baseline 256GB model and going up to $3,199 for 2TB. But if you're eager to change how you use your phone every day, the sheer power of this multitasking engine has me convinced that the future of Apple's mobile platform is unfolding right before our eyes. In 2014, I began my career at PCMag as a freelancer. That blossomed into a full-time position in 2021, and I now review email marketing apps, mobile operating systems, web hosting services, streaming music platforms, and video games as a senior writer. I'm a graduate of Hunter College, a hard-core gamer, and an Apple enthusiast.

item.title: SALES: Anker’s new USB-C hub packs 10 ports and a smart display for just $80
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
A USB-C hub adds extra ports for hooking up to monitors, storage devices, and other peripherals. Docking stations, however, are especially useful for fixed workstations, as they replace adaptors and minimize the need to swap cables. Right now, you can get the Anker Nano 10-in-1 USB-C hub (with Smart Display) for just $79.99 on Amazon. That’s 20 percent off of the $99.99 MSRP. This is the first time we’re seen the price drop since September. Until now, we’ve just seen it at full price. The Anker hub combines 10 ports in compact housing measuring 13 x 5 x 5.6 centimeters. These include HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, USB-C with up to 10 Gbit/s, USB-A with up to 10 Gbit/s, two further USB-A ports, each with up to five Gbit/s, Gigabit Ethernet, and both SD and microSD card readers compliant with the 3.0 standard. This allows you to connect monitors, a mouse, a keyboard, external drives, and memory cards to a single device. That said, it doesn’t feature a separate audio output. For video output, the hub supports a monitor with up to 4K at 144 Hertz or 2K at 240 Hertz. Alternatively, you can use two screens up to 2K and 240 Hertz. The maximum performance depends on the laptop’s specifications and the connected monitors. Video output is via HDMI and DisplayPort only. The hub does not support USB-C monitors. There’s an integrated smart display at the front of the device. It shows the status of the ports, the charging power, the data transfer rate, and the device temperature in real time. You can also upload your own images and view them in a slideshow. A customizable focus timer helps you structure your work sessions. You can even adjust the display settings and the 25-minute focus timer via the web dashboard. The accompanying app allows you to start photo slideshows and install firmware updates. Around 80 percent of the ports face backwards, which allows you to route cables to the rear or downwards. The permanent host cable connects the hub to the laptop and offers some flexibility in terms of placement. For power supply, the hub features a USB-C port with up to 100 watts of Power Delivery. According to the manufacturer, up to 80 watts of this is available for charging the connected laptop. Anker doesn’t supply a suitable power adaptor, though. For optimum performance, the manufacturer recommends a USB-C charger with at least 65 watts. Without an external power supply, the laptop powers the hub, ensuring that its basic functions remain available. The front USB-C port and USB-A ports are for data transfer only, which means they’re not suitable for charging or video output. Anker lists Windows 10, Windows 11, and macOS as compatible operating systems. On macOS, two connected external monitors display the same screen content. According to the manufacturer, displaying different content on both screens is only possible on Windows. The hub does not support Linux. For $79.99, you get a docking station that combines multiple ports into a single device and displays additional information on its smart display. This makes it particularly appealing to anyone who regularly uses a laptop at a desk, connects multiple monitors, or transfers data from memory cards. Reviews (so far) have praised the wide range of ports and the solid build quality. Several buyers highlight the display, the magnetic stand, and the ability to connect monitors, network devices, and peripherals to a single device. The rear-facing port panel and the braided, permanently attached cable are also well received. There are, however, some limitations: One user criticizes the lack of an audio output and the restriction to Gigabit Ethernet. Others point out that achieving high refresh rates depends on the technical specifications of the laptop. Mac users should also expect the two external screens to display the same image. Another user notes that the permanently attached cable cannot be easily replaced if it fails. The lack of a power supply unit may also incur additional costs. This laptop feels like it was made for real life. It’s just a good balance of the stuff that matters. The 16-inch 2560×1600 IPS screen gives you more room for viewing long documents. The battery life is also good enough to get you through most of the school day. Plus, having 1TB of storage means you don’t have to constantly delete things to make room. The biggest thing to think about here is size. A 16-inch laptop is perfect when you’re sitting at a desk, but toss it in a bag and you’ll start to feel the weight of it in your shoulder. It’s not the heaviest machine at just over four pounds, but it’s definitely not the lightest. Also know, this isn’t a gaming laptop. It can handle a good amount of things, but 3D work and heavy video editing may be outside of its range. But as a general purpose tool for school chores and other matters, this laptop delivers the goods with the backing of the Dell brand and build quality. HP OmniBook 3: Best HP laptop for students Who is the HP OmniBook 3 for? Hang on. While we haven’t reviewed the HP OmniBook 3 ourselves, we still think it earns a spot here because you’re getting a large display and ample storage for a price you just can’t argue with (just a little over $500 at the time of this writing). The 1920×1080 display measures 17.3-inches, and that’s a lot of space for multitasking or scrolling through long (densely written) documents. But the 512GB SSD is a big selling point here because it’s more than you’d find in most entry-level machines. Toss in the Ryzen 3 CPU and you’ve got yourself something decent. Sure, we wish it had more than 8GB of RAM–that’s the bare minimum we’d ever accept. Just remember that this laptop’s meant for lighter workloads, not demanding ones. If you are mostly interested in research, writing papers, browsing the web, email, and enjoying media, this is an affordable option for students. Acer Chromebook Plus 514: Best Chromebook for students Who should buy the Acer Chromebook Plus 514? If your needs are fairly basic (checking e-mail or scrolling through reddit), the Acer Chromebook Plus 514 is a compelling option and I’ll tell you why. For one, the 14-inch keyboard feels good for typing, with large keys and a good amount of space between them. The IPS touch-enabled display also offers a functional 1920×1080 resolution and a 60Hz refresh rate, all pretty typical for a Chromebook in this price range. Its Intel i3-N305 processor has eight cores, which is sufficient for things like web chores and Google’s suite of productivity apps. Normally, Chromebooks offer meager storage because it’s web-based. But this model is surprisingly generous with 512GB of storage. That’s worth some attention right there. Acer Chromebook Plus 514: Further considerations It’s not the prettiest-looking machine in the world. In fact, it’s pretty utilitarian. The chassis is also made of plastic, so it’s not going to be as sturdy as aluminum builds. Still, it a good laptop for the money. You’ve got to be comfortable using only Google, though. The PCWorld team puts Windows laptops through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and so on. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and compare it against others we’ve tested. Chromebooks, on the other hand, go through a series of web-based tests. For a much deeper look at our review methodology, check out how PCWorld tests laptops. Who curated this article? Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo, and I oversee all laptop and home robotics coverage here at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also deeply immersed in the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are heading next. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a good book, or hanging out with my greyhound. How to choose the best laptop for college First off, think about your budget. What’s your actual limit here? If you don’t have much wiggle room, a Chromebook might be the way to go. They’re cheap and can handle everyday tasks like writing papers and casual browsing. That sort of thing. You can find them anywhere from $200 to about a grand, it just depends on what you’re going for. Laptop prices on Amazon can change at the drop of a hat, so go slow and compare configurations carefully. Don’t just go for the cheapest option. If you’ve got a little more to spend, 2-in-1 touchscreen laptops are great because they’re so versatile. You can turn the screen all the way back and use it like a tablet or stand it up like a little movie screen. That’s great for Netflix or just zoning out with YouTube. The flexibility’s nice, especially if you’re cramped in a dorm or carrying it around all the time. As far as performance goes, if you’re doing stuff like email, streaming, or having a bunch of tabs open, more RAM helps. 8GB is what I’d recommend. Your laptop will run smoother and it won’t feel like it’s constantly lagging. 4GB is fine if you’re just browsing or writing papers, but it can feel restrictive if you’re prone to multitasking and working with lots of open windows. Chrome and Spotify are memory hogs as well, and they’ll slow things down if you don’t have enough memory to work with. Last thing, the keyboard. You’ll be typing a lot in college, so this actually matters. Some people like keys that are clickier and have a little more bounce to them. Well, that’s mechanical keyboards for you. They’re louder, but they help you avoid accidental keystrokes, and they feel kind of satisfying to type on. Totally up to you, but don’t ignore it. A bad keyboard gets old real fast. What’s the best laptop for college students? The Acer Swift 16 AI is the most well-rounded pick because it offers a strong balance of performance, portability, and battery life. What’s the best budget laptop for college students? The MacBook Neo is PCWorld’s leading budget pick. It packs Apple’s A19 Pro chip, which delivers plenty of speed for schoolwork and browsing, and a gorgeous 13-inch Liquid Retina display plus a premium aluminum design. What’s the difference between a Chromebook and a Windows laptop? Chromebooks are simple and fast, perfect for stuff like browsing, writing papers, and streaming. They do everything within the ChromeOS. They usually don’t cost much, either. Windows laptops can do a lot more like gaming or editing videos. They also support locally installed programs as opposed to being internet-based. So if you just need a basic laptop for school stuff, a Chromebook is cool, but if you want something that can handle more, go with Windows.

item.title: REVIEW: Plucky Chinese startup claims to beat Nvidia DGX Spark, Mac Mini on Qwen — says its '256 TOPS beats 1000 TOPS in prefill', running 16-core Cortex-A55 SoC on 40w
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
- Sipeed claims its 256 TOPS mini PC can outperform Nvidia on Qwen - The 128GB Sipeed MaixStation costs less than Nvidia's reported $6,949 DGX Spark - Nvidia advertises 1,000 sparse FP4 TOPS, while Sipeed emphasizes practical inference performance Chinese electronics manufacturer Sipeed has claimed its upcoming MaixStation AI computer can outperform Nvidia's DGX Spark in certain Qwen workloads despite considerably lower advertised computing performance. Powered by Axera's AX8860P processor, the compact machine combines 16 Arm Cortex-A55 cores with AI acceleration reaching 256 TOPS and typical consumption of 40W. Sipeed is also challenging Apple's Mac Mini in its comparisons, although the available benchmark figures primarily concern Nvidia's system rather than Apple's hardware. MaixStation challenges Nvidia's performance advantage Sipeed's published Qwen results indicate that its 128GB configuration slightly exceeds the DGX Spark's performance, with further software improvements expected to increase throughput. The company attributes this outcome partly to differences in how advertised computing capacity translates into actual performance when processing large language models. Nvidia advertises 1,000 TOPS using sparse FP4 calculations, whereas Sipeed argues that practical workloads cannot fully exploit this theoretical computing capability. Although Nvidia's dense FP4 performance approaches 500 TOPS theoretically, Sipeed maintains that its architecture uses available processing resources more efficiently during prefill. Both machines offer 273GB/s memory bandwidth, although Sipeed claims architectural optimizations allow its processor to sustain higher utilization during demanding inference operations. The comparisons were conducted with speculative decoding through multi-token prediction disabled, allowing the company to evaluate both systems under similar conditions. However, the reported advantage remains relatively small, and independent testing would be necessary to establish performance differences across additional models and workloads. The AX8860P uses a 6nm manufacturing process, supports 256-bit LPDDR5X memory and provides PCIe 5.0 connectivity alongside Axera's proprietary AXLink interconnect. Its specifications also include 64 video decoding channels, 16 encoding channels and support for configurations containing as much as 128GB memory. Sipeed expects its entry-level MaixStation with 32GB memory to cost below $2,000, while the 128GB configuration should remain under $4,000. By comparison, Nvidia's DGX Spark reportedly sells for $6,949.99, considerably above its original $3,000 to $4,000 pricing announced during March 2025. The compact AI mini PC measures 110 × 110 × 30 mm and includes USB 3.0 Type-C connectivity alongside a 10GbE SFP+ network interface. Although normal consumption is approximately 40W, the computer receives electricity through a 65W USB Power Delivery connection using its Type-C port. Sipeed claims its 32GB model supports Qwen3.8-27B, while a 128GB configuration can accommodate the considerably larger Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 125B model. Combining two units provides 256GB memory for DeepSeek V4-Flash 284B, while a four-unit MaixStation Pro configuration offers 512GB for DeepSeek V4.1-Flash 552B. AXLink supports communication between processors, with Axera claiming approximately 80% interconnect efficiency when multiple chips operate within connected computing systems. Software compatibility reportedly includes PyTorch, ONNX, vLLM, SGLang and Hugging Face formats, alongside interfaces compatible with OpenAI applications and Axera's development tools. The company plans a Kickstarter campaign within several months, offering prospective customers a $100 discount through a reservation costing $30. Despite its claimed advantages, commercial availability, final pricing, and independently verified performance remain unresolved, particularly for configurations running extremely large language models.

item.title: REVIEW: JBL Bar 800MK2 review: awesome Atmos and surround sound in one package
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Despite skipping on up-firing drivers, the JBL Bar 800MK2 plates up spectacularly expansive sound with its virtual Dolby Atmos capabilities. Its thumping bass and clear dialogue are impressive too, as are its wide connectivity options and feature-rich companion app. It isn’t the flashiest of lookers, and the sub is on the bulky side, but the ingenious detachable surround speakers almost sell this model on their own, and the system is easy to recommend now that it’s regularly discounted. - +Excellent performance across the frequency range - +Strong feature-set and connectivity options - -Lacks up-firing speakers for true Atmos - -HDMI input supports 4K, but only at 60Hz Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The JBL Bar 800MK2 is the mid-range option in the audio specialist’s MK2 line, delivering surround sound though its main bar, detachable rear speakers, and mighty subwoofer. It comes with Dolby Atmos and DTS:X support, a wide range of connectivity options, and an expansive 7.1 channel configuration — but is it actually worth buying? I’ve spent a bunch of hours testing the JBL Bar 800MK2 for myself, putting it to the test with 4K UHD Blu-rays as well as Dolby Atmos and stereo format music. Here’s whether I’d recommend it or not. Let’s start by talking about performance, an area where this model certainly excels. Like a lot of the best soundbars, the JBL Bar 800MK2 produces beautifully expansive sound with powerful bass and clear dialogue, and it consistently impressed me during testing. It makes use of six full-range drivers and two tweeters in the main bar, two full rangers in each surround speaker, and a ten-inch bass unit in the sub, with a solid 780W maximum power output, so you’re really going to feel the action in every scene when watching movies. For instance, when watching a 4K Blu-ray of The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, I was blown away by the thunderous bass on offer as a UFO airlifted Peach’s Castle into the stratosphere, with a regimented, rippling sound emanating from the sub. As the chaos unfurled, crashing waves hit with tremendous impact, and as Toads jumped into the water, their movement was tracked with commendable precision. Similarly, the sound of Yoshi’s tongue flicking across the scene was mapped perfectly, making for an immensely immersive viewing experience, with the width of his motion far exceeding the limited confines of the soundbar. The JBL Bar 800MK2 skips on dedicated up-firing drivers, so you’re not going to get the most convincing verticality while watching Atmos movies, but I was still seriously impressed with the virtual recreation of height effects. For example, in Top Gun Maverick, the sound of Tom Cruise flying a jet up and overhead sounded surprisingly life-like, and it genuinely seemed as if I could hear the upward trajectory. The low-end rumble of jet engines also shook our testing room to its foundations, but all the while, dialogue continued to come through clearly in the mix. Speaking of dialogue, the JBL Bar 800MK2 is well equipped to deliver clear and concise speech at all times. That’s in part thanks to the PureVoice setting, which enables you to push vocals forward without ruining the fidelity of sounds elsewhere in the frequency range. I never felt like PureVoice made the movie’s audio seem unbalanced, and it proved to be super-effective, especially in more crowded, action-packed sequences where dialogue can sometimes take a backseat. I was also really impressed with the sound quality coming from the detachable rear speakers. They sounded brilliantly balanced from where I was sitting, but you can easily change their volume level in the JBL One app to suit your room setup. They gave Dolby Atmos movies an ultra-expansive quality, and provided controlled highs and clear mids, making for stellar surround sound. Even when it came to music, the JBL Bar 800MK2 performed fantastically well. With an Atmos mix of Stayin’ Alive by the Bee Gees, the system whipped up a strikingly expansive presentation with articulate drums in the treble range, great vocal clarity, and warm bass that never sounded overly assertive. The rears also combined really nicely here, which was a relief as I’ve found that the surround channels on some rival models don't always seem cohesive with the rest of the system. Stereo music impressed me too, with deep and agile bass, detailed mids, and solid instrument separation. So yes, despite lacking dedicated up-firing drivers, the virtual Atmos on the 800MK2 works very well, and it handles the fundamentals with ease too. But how does this model fare elsewhere? In terms of features, this system is a strong all-rounder. On top of the PureVoice setting I mentioned, there’s a Night Mode that uses the detachable speakers only, voice assistant support, AirPlay and Google Cast support, EQ options, and much more. All of these features can be tapped into over on the JBL One app, which is intuitive and incredibly easy to use. There are a few sound-related features I’d like to highlight too. The first is MultiBeam 3.0, which is intended to create a “wide, cinema-like soundstage”. This feature harnesses beamforming and digital processing to achieve its goal, and works a treat. There’s also a sound calibration option, which is quick and seamless, and provides optimized three-dimensional sound for your space, no matter how it’s set up. The Bar 800MK2 also has a very solid set of connectivity options. You get the usual HDMI eARC, digital optical, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth, but also Ethernet and an HDMI input (just one, rather than the three on the Bar 1300MK2). The HDMI input supports 4K passthrough, but only at 60Hz, so it's not the best option if you’re looking for peak-performance gaming or anything. Before we wrap up, I also want to talk about design. On the one hand, the JBL Bar 800MK2 is ingenious. Its use of battery powered rear speakers makes it incredibly versatile. You can place these anywhere in your room for a flexible, wire-free setup, and the speakers can even function as standalone Bluetooth speakers. If they run low on charge, they can even be used while connected to a USB-C power cable. That alone is a huge plus. But that’s actually where my praise runs dry. The JBL Bar 800MK2 looks quite cheap for the price you pay, with a plasticky one-note appearance. The sub is also very bulky — even more so than the more powerful alternative you get with the JBL Bar 1300MK2. But then again, what the system lacks in style, it certainly makes up for in substance. When all’s said and done, is the JBL Bar 800MK2 worth the money? Well, its list price of £899 / AU$1,199.95 (about $1,200) may seem steep, but realistically, you’ll be paying less than £650 / AU$850 for it now. At that price, the Bar 800MK2 is well worth it. Despite its bulk and lack of up-firing drivers, it's an excellent performer with incredible virtual Atmos and low-end might, as well as a top-class feature-set and versatile connectivity options. Want something more slim and stylish? Then I’d recommend scooping up the new Sonos Beam Ultra and building out a system at your own pace. But if you want a great value surround sound package, look no further than the JBL Bar 800MK2. JBL Bar 800MK2 review: price & release date - Priced at £899 / AU$1,199.95 (about $1,200) The JBL Bar 800MK2 was released in June 2025 as part of the refreshed MK2 line, alongside the smaller Bar 300MK2 as well as the larger 1000MK2 and 1300MK2. The JBL Bar 800MK2 is priced at £899 / AU$1,199.95 (about $1,200), but can often be found on sale for less than £650 / AU$850. It appears that the soundbar system is still unavailable for purchase in the US, unfortunately. Should I buy the JBL Bar 800MK2? You want almighty sound for movie nights The JBL Bar 800MK2 plates up phenomenally powerful, cinematic sound, packing plenty of bass and expansive Dolby Atmos. If you want massive audio for immersive movie-watching, this is a great option. You’re looking for a soundbar with flexible surrounds The battery powered surround speakers that come with the JBL Bar 800MK2 are excellent. They sound fantastic, can easily slot onto the main bar to charge up, and don’t require wires when in use. You can even use them as standalone Bluetooth speakers, meaning that their versatility is unmatched. The JBL Bar 800MK2 lacks dedicated up-firing speakers, meaning that it has to rely on virtual processing to replicate Dolby Atmos content. While the Bar 800MK’s virtual Atmos is genuinely impressive, the larger JBL Bar 1300MK2 should be your go-to for premium spatial sound. The JBL Bar 800MK2 isn’t much of a looker. Its build quality could be better for the price, and the sub seems oversized, especially given that the more powerful 1300MK2 offers a more compact bass unit. At a glance, this model may seem far too expensive to compete with the Bar 800MK2, but I often see it on sale for close to the JBL’s launch price. This is the ultimate surround sound package, with top-tier cinematic sound, excellent connectivity options, an 11.1.4 channel configuration, and both Dolby Atmos and DTS:X support. Up-firing drivers mean you get true Atmos, and HDMI passthrough is on board for ultimate ease of use. Read our full Samsung HW-Q990H review. The Sonos Beam Ultra is a totally different proposition, but it’s fully worth your consideration. This model has up-firing drivers, incredible bass output, and crystal-clear dialogue, making it amazing for both movies and music. It doesn’t come with a sub or surrounds, but these can be added easily through the Sonos app when purchased separately. This model is more compact, and looks beautiful to boot, so if you’re OK with building out a system of your own rather than getting a pre-built combo, it’s my top recommendation. Read my full Sonos Beam Ultra review. - Assessed at our TV testing space at Future Labs - Used 4K Blu-ray for movies and Tidal Connect to stream music - One of more than 30 soundbars I’ve tested I spent many hours using the JBL Bar 800MK2 for watching movies and listening to music. I judged its capabilities at our TV testing space at Future Labs, made use of all of the soundbar’s features, and tried it with multiple surround speaker configurations. Most of the time, I used HDMI eARC to connect the LG G6 OLED TV, and watched 4K Blu-ray discs via the Panasonic DP-UB820 to assess the soundbar’s handling of Dolby Atmos movies. I did, however, also test the Bar 800MK2 with Netflix movies, and used Tidal Connect to stream music over Wi-Fi. More generally, I’ve tested more than 30 soundbars during my time here at TechRadar, where I serve as a Senior Reviews Writer. I’ve reviewed everything from budget-friendly bars like the Sony HT-SF150 through to huge surround sound systems such as the Bar 800MK2’s big sibling, the JBL Bar 1300MK2.
