item.title: REVIEW: Deepseek's latest AI model is smarter than ever, but its low running costs come at a price
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
Deepseek just upgraded its V4.1 Flash open-weight model to revision 1017. What looks like a mere point revision may actually be a significant step forward in model efficiency. On the product page, Deepseek uses the slogan "wish-driven programming made real," a likely reference to the colloquial "vibe coding," implying the model is a good fit for open-ended tasks with broad descriptions. However, while the model is indeed cheap and scores well, it can be hallucination-prone. LLMs are roughly divided into two categories: closed commercial efforts from frontier labs, whose models are expensive to run but deliver excellent results, and Chinese open-weight competitors that broadly exchange reliability for a much cheaper running cost, particularly for long-running agentic tasks. Deepseek V4.1 Flash (DSF) is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 552B total parameters, 16B of which are active during runs. The model is multimodal, accepts both text and images as inputs, and its context window length measures the now-standard 1 million tokens. According to Deepseek's internal benchmarks, the model slots in neatly between GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5, even beating Anthropic's LLM in task tests. That's already a strong showing, but this latest revision of DSF shines in the performance-per-task base and token efficiency. The upgrade from V4 Flash to V4.1 Flash significantly slashed hardware requirements, with V4.1 using only one-quarter of the HBM and one-eighth of SSD storage for its KV cache compared to its predecessor, spending only 890 bytes per token entry. The company illustrates the point with a cost-per-task graph based on DeepSWE's dataset from September 2, adding its own data points for both DSF and DSF-1017. Both variants cluster in the desirable top-left area, and even low-effort runs of DSF-1017 offer a task completion rate in the ballpark of "max" settings for pricey competitors. It's worth noting that DeepSWE is only one of many benchmarks, but this is nonetheless an impressive result. Even at Deepseek's own pricing (remember, this is an open-weight model you can run anywhere), the price at off-peak times per million tokens is just $0.15 for input and $0.6 for output. On cache hits, the input token cost drops to a mere $0.003. It's worth keeping in mind that third-party providers have undercut Deepseek API in the past, so those figures could go lower if you shop around inference providers. Deepseek also offers search functionality at $0.75 per 1,000 queries, an amount that undercuts competitors, with the closest one being Parallel at $1. DeepSWE isn't the only benchmark around, either. Artificial Analysis ranks DSF-1017 (max) as only #2 on its intelligence index within the large open-weight class, with a score of 45. For reference, the most seemingly intelligent model, Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback), rings in at 58. It's one of the fastest models in its category, too, and its cost-per-task is edged out only by Xiaomi's MiMo V2.6-Pro. This all sounds too good to be true, but everyone knows the adage of "fast, cheap, and reliable, pick two." So what's the catch? In one word: hallucination. Just because a model is smart doesn't mean it's reliable. Broadly speaking, users prefer models that don't answer when they lack supporting facts, and DSF-1017 doesn't seem very good at knowing what it doesn't know. Artificial Analysis' Omniscience benchmark is quite clear on this matter, ranking the model among the lowest. It answered questions correctly 43% of the time, which is among the best for open-weight models, but inferior to the proprietary competition. That would be perfectly acceptable if it skipped answers without a foundation, but it hallucinated 67% of non-answers. The benchmark's main index grants points for good answers and deducts them for wrong ones, and non-answers don't count. DSF-1017 gets 5 points, compared to Kimi K3-max's 20, with the frontier models coming in at 42+. Ultimately, this means DFS-1017 is by no means incompetent — much the opposite —but one should be careful about which tasks to assign to the model. Tasks with verifiable outputs like programming, OCR with review, and format conversions will be fine, as the agent can run verification steps against its work and try again. However, open-ended research, looking up facts, and interpreting or drafting highly precise documents are tasks better suited to a frontier model — or, you know, a human — as hallucinations likely won't be properly reined in and results won't be very trustworthy. "Fast and loose" seems to be a forming trend for highly competent open-weight models, too. Several months ago, when Kimi K3 was released, everyone raved about how effective and cheap it was, and how it proposed to offer frontier-level intelligence for a fraction of the price. My personal experience with Kimi was short-lived, as even short but precise fact look-ups came up with hallucinated information, and Artificial Analysis' data seems to back this observation up. Nevertheless, open-weight models remain important both to make AI agents more accessible in absolute dollar terms and potentially as a tool to drive down the cost of intelligence when facing down potential price rises from frontier labs.

item.title: REVIEW: Khadas Mind Pro mini PC review
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The innovative design of the Khadas Mind Pro with the modular expansion options really appeals to me. Inside is an innovative standby battery and a modular design that can make use of a plugin dock and eGPU, making it ideal for photographers, content creators and professionals. It does come at a huge price, but delivers impressive performance in Photoshop, Lightroom, Microsoft Office and 4K video editing. The limited Thunderbolt connectivity and GPU power without the optional extras mean that you have to really need that compact size and portability to justify it. - -Midweight Local LLM without accessories Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Having reviewed the Khadas Mind 2S just over a year ago, I was impressed by just how much processing power Khadas had managed to squeeze into such a small machine. Now, with the arrival of the Mind Pro, the company has retained much the same compact form factor and innovative modular design, while introducing Intel’s latest Core Ultra processor and Arc integrated graphics. The result is an exceptionally powerful mini PC that feels just as capable as many considerably larger desktop systems, especially when it comes to everyday productivity as well as creative applications. It once again features the premium metal construction, and with dimensions of just 146 × 105 × 28mm, it’s small enough to slip into a bag and carry between home and office. What makes this particularly useful is the integrated 7.98Wh standby battery, which allows the machine to maintain your Windows session while moving between those locations, much the same as using a laptop. During testing, I was able to leave applications open, disconnect the computer, throw the Khadas Mind Pro in my backpack and travel home. Then I was able to reconnect to a monitor, mouse and keyboard at home and continue the session without needing to re-open applications and work. This is what we have come to expect from laptops, but not with a Mini PC, and it’s a surprisingly useful feature, boosted by the option of extras such as the Dock and GPU modules. Performance is equally impressive as it features an Intel Core Ultra X7 358H, combined with 64GB of RAM and integrated Arc B390 graphics. This combination proved to handle Microsoft Office, Photoshop and Lightroom extremely well. Even Adobe Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve proved more usable than I had anticipated with 4K footage shot on the GoPro Mission 1 ILS. Gaming was another surprise, with Cyberpunk 2077 and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle both running at medium-quality settings; although as I extended play there were occasional frame drops, there was nothing too much to impact gameplay. The other point here was that the fans kicked in and, while audible, they remained relatively quiet. The machine also has considerable AI potential, with a dedicated NPU and 64GB of shared memory. My initial CPU-based Lemonade AI testing showed that it could handle practical local AI tasks, although switching between models wasn’t always straightforward. Using the dedicated NPU with the right models gained some impressive results, but again selecting the right LLM manager and model takes some time, this process took me from Lemonade to the LM Studio. Through the test, my main issue with the machine was the connectivity. With only two Thunderbolt 4 ports, it’s easy to run out of high-speed connections when using a USB-C monitor, power supply and external storage. If you are using the Mind Pro as your main desktop, this is where the optional Mind Dock starts to make sense and is more like an essential purchase. Ultimately, the Mind Pro is an impressive example of innovation and how far mini PCs have progressed. It won't be the best mini PC for most users. It isn’t cheap, and you’ll need to invest further to see the full potential of its modular design, but the impressive processing power, portability and modular extras make it expensive but very desirable. - Where can you get it? Directly from Khadas The Khadas Mind Pro costs $2,599 for the Core Ultra X7 358H, 64GB RAM and 2TB SSD configuration that I’ve looked at in this review and is available directly from Khadas. Alongside the Mini PC, you can also purchase the optional Mind Dock, Mind xPlay and Mind Graphics 2, although these will add considerably to the overall cost. CPU: Intel Core Ultra X7 358H, 16 cores / 16 threads Graphics: Intel Arc B390 integrated graphics NPU: Intel AI Boost NPU 5, up to 50 TOPS Additional storage: M.2 2230 NVMe expansion slot Rear Ports: 2 x Thunderbolt 4, 2× USB-A 3.2 Gen 2, HDMI 2.1 FRL Expansion: Khadas Mind Link proprietary modular interface Audio: Audio output via supported display, USB and compatible expansion accessories. Battery: 7.98Wh internal standby battery Optional Accessories: Mind Dock, Mind xPlay and Mind Graphics 2 Unpacking the compact AX9 Max, the metal casing and detailed plastic base of this mini PC instantly reinforced its price point. Only after carefully checking the detailing and the large, shiny logo on top did I start to question whether this was a premium machine or just one trying to look premium. Checking the specifications and that the price point was justified, but there’s still something about the design that feels a little over the top. The rest of the design is solid, and at 134.9 × 131.8 × 57.7mm and 777.5g, it’s a great size and weight for this style of machine. Around the casing, there are four USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports and a 3.5mm stereo headphone jack. On the left side of the casing is an SD 4.0 memory card slot, while the back has two USB4 Type-C ports, a USB 2.0 port, two HDMI 2.1 ports, two 2.5Gb RJ45 sockets, a USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A port, and the DC-in port. Having reviewed the Khadas Mind 2S just over a year ago, I was impressed by the combination of its exceptionally small size, processing power and innovative modular design. With the arrival of the Mind Pro, it’s immediately apparent that the company has retained much of the ethos of those initial machines and what made them so interesting. The form factor is familiar, the design remains incredibly minimalist, and once again, it’s the modular expansion ecosystem that differentiates this from the usual mini PCs I look at. The first impression is that this is an exceptionally well-made and small mini PC. The metal casing gives it a premium feel, with solid construction, and it’s just understated when it comes to styling, which I really like. The front just features the power button mounted into a subtle cutaway, and all connectivity options are lined up at the rear. The compact dimensions are great if you have limited desk space or you need to take the machine between locations. This portability is one of the key features and, like a laptop that enables you to close the lid without powering down, the Mind Pro enable you to do much the same when you move from one location to another. Simply unplug the monitor, keyboard and mouse, and pop it in your bag; then, when you get to the next location, connect up and off you go. All the apps and work that you were working on will still be there and ready for you to continue with. The idea behind the machine is that you have the core, which is the Mind Pro, then you have the accessories, so in the office where you need to focus on high-demand work, you’ll have the Mind Graphics 2 eGPU Module and Mind Dock All-In-One Docking Station. While at home, where you may just want to check email and do some light work, you may just need the Mind xPlay Portable Display + Keyboard, which will, in low-power mode, essentially give you the same abilities as a Windows Home laptop. You can also plug in the Tone2 for audio. The point is the Mind Pro is just the core, and how and where you use it will dictate what additional extras you want and need. What makes the portability possible is the integrated 7.98Wh standby battery. This isn’t designed primarily to power the machine in the same way as a laptop battery and instead is used to maintain the machine's working state when disconnected from external power. Taking a look at the limited ports on the back, there are two Thunderbolt 4 ports, an HDMI 2.1 connection and two USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 ports. While this matches most premium laptops, I found that the two Thunderbolt connections became a bit of an issue, particularly when using the Mind Pro for creative work. With a Thunderbolt monitor and power connected, there was no fast connection left for connecting high-speed external SSDs or card readers without using an additional adapter. The two USB-A connections are useful, but their 10Gbps maximum transfer rate is far slower than the Thunderbolt 4’s 40Gbps connection bandwidth. Considering the performance on offer here, a third Thunderbolt connection would have been welcome. For anyone intending to use the Mind Pro as their main desktop computer, the Mind Dock is essential, and at $199, that's quite an additional cost on an already expensive machine. The all-metal construction does make the Mind Pro look like it should be passively cooled. However, there is an active cooling system inside, and while the fans become audible on many of the more demanding tasks, I was generally well controlled. During intensive creative work, the casing also became warm to the touch, which isn’t particularly surprising given the amount of processing power packed into such a small space. The design of this small machine is stunning, and the portability of the design with the integrated standby battery is actually a great idea. However, when it comes to the design, the limited port selection is frustrating, especially at this price, but it has been designed to be used as a modular setup, and the dock and GPU are available to boost the performance further at a cost. The Khadas Mind Pro builds on the modular design of the machines that I have looked at in the past from the company and combines powerful processing with a proprietary expansion interface and an integrated standby battery. At the heart of the system is Intel’s Core Ultra X7 358H, a 16-core processor supported by Intel Arc B390 integrated graphics and a dedicated AI Boost NPU. In this review, I have looked at the standard Pro machine with 64GB of LPDDR5X memory and a 2TB PCIe 4.0 SSD. While those specifications are impressive, what separates this from most other mini PCs is that it has been designed so that the Mind Pro can easily move between different work and home environments, with a range of Mind Link connection expansion modules that adapt its use depending on your needs. These modules include the Mind Dock that provides additional connectivity for when it’s used as a desktop workstation, and this comes in at around $200. Then there's the Mind xPlay portable display at $99, or with keyboard at $399, which offers a more mobile configuration. There’s also the Mind Graphics 2 that adds dedicated graphics processing for creative applications, gaming and potentially supported AI workloads, and this will set you back a further $1449. Unfortunately, none of these modules was available during my testing, so I wasn’t able to assess the complete ecosystem. Even without the expansion options, however, the Mind Pro has plenty of raw processing power. The internal 7.98Wh battery is the most unique, and as I found this on a normal working day when I regularly travel between office, home and college, with a journey time that can vary from ten minutes up to an hour and a half. With a conventional mini PC, that would mean saving everything, closing applications and shutting down before leaving, then re-opening everything when I get to my next destination. Which is one of the reasons I use a laptop, as I can keep everything open; however, the laptop isn’t light. With the Mind Pro, I could simply disconnect the power, place the machine in my backpack and reconnect it at the other end, just like a laptop, just minus the screen, keyboard, and trackpad. Throughout testing, this worked exceptionally well. I could leave Adobe Premiere Pro and other applications open, move between locations and return to the same Windows session without having to reopen everything. It certainly makes for a lightweight alternative, although the internal 2TB SSD provides plenty of space for applications and smaller projects; I generally edit video from external storage. This makes the portable workflow slightly more complicated, as unplugging an external SSD while Premiere Pro is accessing footage isn’t particularly advisable, but then that’s the same on a laptop. For shorter productions, however, the system really comes into its own. During testing, I was editing approximately five-minute videos using footage from the GoPro Mission One, with the files stored directly on the internal SSD. This enabled me to start editing at the office, disconnect the computer and finish the project at home without closing Premiere Pro or shutting down Windows. The battery also allows the Mind Pro to operate independently of external power for short periods, although this is very much a secondary feature. Using the Khadas Mind app, it’s possible to select the Use Battery option under Device Mode When Unplugged, allowing the computer to continue operating instead of immediately entering a standby state. To see how practical this was, I tested the machine using three power settings, with a mixture of Microsoft Word, web browsing and Adobe Lightroom. At maximum power, the system lasted approximately seven minutes before displaying a low-battery warning and entering its low-power state. Switching to the medium power setting in the Mind application was able to extend this working time to around 14 minutes, while the lowest power setting was around 30 minutes. These figures are far less than the 60 minutes quoted by Khadas for light active use. Most importantly, this internal battery feature means the machine wasn’t losing my work when the battery ran low. Cinebench R23 CPU Multi (Threads): 20,252 Cinebench R23 CPU Single (Threads): 2,084 Cinebench 2026 CPU Multi (Threads): 4,835 Cinebench 2026 CPU Single (Threads): 505 Getting started with the Khadas Mind Pro follows the usual process, and the machine arrives with Windows 11 Home preinstalled, alongside the Khadas Mind software, and the initial Windows setup takes around 10 to 15 minutes. Aside from the usual process of accepting or declining Microsoft’s various additional services, there is very little to do before you’re up and running. Then the Khadas Mind application provides access to the machine’s power management and battery options, highlighting that this is far more than a normal mini PC. While the modular ecosystem enables you to expand the system with a docking station or external GPU, even as the core unit when used as a standalone computer, the Mind Pro offers impressive performance, especially considering its small size. I started the test by installing Microsoft Office; there was more than enough performance to run Word, Excel and PowerPoint all at the same time, alongside multiple browser windows. Everything remained fast and responsive, and even when adding Photoshop and Lightroom into the mix, there was little indication that the system was struggling. As is now common, there’s also a dedicated Intel NPU, and that adds potential for supported local AI features, although cloud-based Microsoft Copilot functionality shouldn’t be confused with processing directly on the NPU. Opening up the task manager indicates when the NPU comes into play and often as a support role to cloud-based connections and some app integration. After seeing that standard office applications were well within the machine's capabilities, I moved on to Adobe’s creative applications, and running these showed just how powerful this machine is even without the boost that the optional modules would obviously offer. Lightroom Classic ran extremely smoothly, opening large catalogues, processing high-resolution photographs and exporting batches of images without difficulty. The internal 2TB SSD also performed well, keeping up with the demands of loading, editing and saving substantial image files. Loading Photoshop and the performance was equally impressive. I worked with high-resolution photographs from the Canon EOS R5 C and Sony A7 IV, and the Mind Pro handled them without any noticeable problems. Opening Adobe Bridge, thumbnails appeared quickly, and I could select batches of up to 30 files and open them in Adobe Camera Raw for editing. If you’re a professional photographer, then the small size of the machine and its portability make it a great option, especially when connected to a large monitor. I also found that the 64GB RAM provided substantial headroom, and with the Arc B390 integrated graphics, all image editing and processing was again well within the machine's abilities. One of the features that I really liked was the ability to plug into my monitor and dock in the office and use the machine as I do with any Mini PC; then, when I headed home, I was able to leave several video projects and other documents open, pop the machine in my bag and then reconnect to another monitor in the home office, with all apps and documents still open and ready to go. The machine in that respect is just like a laptop without the screen and keyboard, of course. The benefit here is that it’s far smaller and lighter, so even more portable than a laptop, especially a laptop with this kind of power. While the performance is good, I did have a connectivity issue. My test monitor uses USB-C rather than HDMI, so connecting the display and power supply occupied both Thunderbolt 4 ports. This left only the two USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 connections for external storage and accessories. While these are rated at 10Gbps, they’re considerably slower than the 40Gbps connection bandwidth offered by Thunderbolt 4. For photographers and videographers using fast external SSDs, the optional Mini Dock would make a difference on this front. When video editing, this machine again proved surprisingly capable and while I initially had reservations about how comfortably a mini PC of this size would handle 4K footage in Adobe Premiere Pro, editing a short five-minute project went well with few problems. There were occasional slowdowns, particularly as the edit became more complex, but the overall workflow was better than I expected. After switching the video editing application to DaVinci Resolve, I found through the edits that the performance was similar. Straightforward 4K timelines were fine, although increasing the complexity of the edit resulted in additional slowdowns, particularly during rendering. This is where an external GPU would potentially make a significant difference, and the Mind Graphics 2 looks like an interesting expansion option if you are planning to use this system for more intensive video production. Although, again, this does come at quite a financial cost. Before moving on to the AI potential, I tried out a few games, and again I was surprised by the ability of the machine. I tested Cyberpunk 2077 and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, and both titles loaded successfully, with no issues with the integrated CPU. At medium graphics settings, gameplay was surprisingly good considering that all the graphics processing was being handled by that integrated Intel Arc B390. While I wouldn’t position the Mind Pro as a replacement for a dedicated gaming PC, the ability to run demanding modern titles on a computer this small is impressive. The final test was to take a closer look at the AI potential of the Khadas Mind Pro, loading Lemonade AI and the Qwen model to see just how capable this compact mini PC was when running AI workloads locally. I started by testing several AI models to code a website, generate images, organise files, recognise image content and handle general chatbot and text-generation tasks. The results were mixed, although the 64GB of RAM provided enough headroom to run some relatively large models locally. One issue with the stability of the Lemonade and the AI process that I came up against was when switching between tasks and therefore LLM models. While there was enough memory to load and run individual models, running two larger models side by side seemed to cause issues and checking Task Manager, it showed the RAM maxing out. Instead, I found myself working through different stages, unloading one model before loading the next. For example, when organising images, I first used PowerShell to create a CSV file containing a list of images before handing that information over to the Qwen model to help manage the files. I then switched to an image recognition model to identify image contents and add the relevant tagging information. For small batches, this worked; however, increasing the count from 20 to 100 images, something between the CPU, Lemonade, and the model kept falling over. Through this process, I also found that switching models wasn't always straightforward. Rather than simply unloading one model and loading another, it was often more reliable to close Lemonade Server completely, restart it and then load the next model. Without restarting, the software could become confused, and the process was noticeably less reliable. For a measurable test, I ran through a batch of 20 images, using the AI tools to assist with basic file organisation and CSV-based content management. Because the workflow involved switching between several models, it was difficult to calculate the total number of tokens used across the entire process. However, during one of the main processing stages, the system recorded a time to first token of 9.08 seconds and generated 1,340 tokens in total. CPU utilisation reached 100%, while RAM usage fluctuated between 60% and 80%, showing the machine was capable of handling the workload but was also being pushed relatively hard. The synthetic AI benchmark results backed up the practical testing, with the Khadas Mind Pro achieving a Procyon AI performance score of 1,485. This highlights that when configured correctly with the AI LLM management software, it will have impressive AI processing capabilities, although the real-world tests highlighted that available memory, model management and workflow optimisation are just as important as raw processing performance. What impressed me most was that all of this was possible on such a small machine without an external GPU. The integrated graphics and 64GB of RAM provide a useful starting point for local AI development, experimentation and lighter production tasks, although experimentation with models and setup is at present a necessity. That said, if you're planning to use the Mind Pro extensively for AI processing, the optional Mind Graphics 2 external GPU will be worth the upgrade. The Khadas Mind Pro is an exceptionally compact and powerful mini PC aimed at professionals, creatives and anyone who needs desktop performance across multiple locations without carrying a laptop. What makes this small machine so versatile is the modular design, although I haven’t tested the additional modules in this review, focusing on the RAW power of the core unit. As it stands, used in isolation, it’s surprisingly powerful and a small and stylish option for use in the office or studio; then, if you do need that boost, it can, at a price, be connected to the optional Mind Dock and Mind Graphics 2 external GPU, transforming it into a far more capable workstation for demanding creative applications, video editing and AI workloads. Likewise at home, simply connect a monitor and keyboard, potentially alongside the Mind xPlay portable display, and you’re ready to continue working, or just the occasional check on email. The solid metal construction gives the Mind Pro a premium feel, and its weight and small size make it easy to carry between locations. More importantly, the integrated standby battery means you can unplug the machine, slip it into your bag and reconnect elsewhere without closing applications or restarting Windows. There are some issues, most notably the limited connectivity without a dock and the integrated GPU’s limitations under heavier workloads. However, the impressive CPU performance, 64GB of RAM and excellent portability do make this a highly versatile and desirable machine. You are paying a premium for the quality of the build, the innovation, and the modular concept, but for professionals who regularly move between workspaces, the Mind Pro offers an attractive alternative to a conventional desktop or laptop. Should I buy the Khadas Mind Pro? Buy it if... The Mind Pro combines impressive performance, compact metal construction, and an integrated standby battery, making it easy to transport between workspaces. You like the idea of a modular workstation. The Mind Dock expands connectivity, while the Mind Graphics 2 external GPU boosts performance for demanding creative workloads. Don't buy it if... You need plenty of ports without buying accessories. Connectivity is limited, especially when using USB-C for both power and a display. The optional Mind Dock starts to feel like an essential purchase. You need serious graphics performance out of the box. The integrated GPU handles lighter workloads, but demanding video editing, gaming and AI tasks will benefit from an external GPU. item.title: SALES: Bird Gawkers Rejoice: Birdbuddy’s New Video Bird Feeder Is Just $100
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
Listen up, birdverts: Birdbuddy just released some new video bird feeders, one of which is the cheapest the company has ever released. Check out the $100 Birdbuddy Nook (and a $160 solar version of the Nook) as well as the $220 Home. The new devices replace the Birdbuddy Pro Solar, a product with similar specs but that went for a whopping $339. Each of the new cameras comes with 2K HDR cameras with a 135-degree field of view (up from 122 degrees on the Pro) and support for both landscape and portrait modes. If you’re not familiar with these gadgets, they’re what they sound like—birdfeeders with not-so-hidden cameras that automatically activate when a creature alights on their perches, giving you a more passive way to enjoy a little light avian voyeurism than your traditional intentional birding. The Home is most similar to the original Pro, featuring a similar, more open perch design with a little overhanging roof and dual solar panels on top, but it otherwise sounds like an improvement in every way. It holds six cups of birdseed, up from 3.8 cups, and features 5GHz Wi-Fi in addition to the 2.4GHz of the Pro, which means it should be more responsive as long as it’s within range of your router’s 5GHz signal. Birdbuddy says the Home is also much faster when it comes to pairing with your phone or waking up to capture those avian goings-on. The Birdbuddy Nook features the same 3.8-cup seed capacity as the older Pro and likewise only uses a slower but longer-range 2.4GHz Wi-Fi radio. And it lacks the adjustable perch extender that lets the Birdbuddy Home accommodate larger birds. Both of the new cameras come with free AI bird identification, which Birdbuddy says can spot 11,000 different species. You have to initiate this manually unless you subscribe to Birdbuddy Premium, which can identify birds automatically. The subscription starts at $70 a year and also adds the ability to name specific birds, unlimited AI chat for bird facts, and more. It’s not all upside, though, as noted by The Verge’s Jennifer Pattison Tuohy. One issue is you now have to bring the whole device in to recharge it—the camera isn’t removable. And despite the technically higher FOV, the new Birdbuddies actually produce narrower video in vertical orientation, and Tuohy found the resulting videos’ color wasn’t quite as vibrant as before. However, the addition of a horizontal orientation means they can offer a much wider FOV when you switch to it. Landscape mode wasn’t an option with the Pro. That said, this isn’t something you tweak in the Birdbuddy app; you have to manually rotate the camera. The new Birdbuddy cameras are available now on Birdbuddy’s website. Fans of the older Pro won’t be able to buy that feeder camera there anymore, but it’s still in stock on Amazon, where it’s discounted to $240, as of this writing.

item.title: REVIEW: Razer Basilisk V4 Pro Review: Tried and true and now with AI
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The Basilisk V4 Pro is a great all-around gaming mouse for gamers who want more functionality than a stripped-down FPS mouse, but who aren't totally button-crazy. - +200 hour battery life; 54 hours at 8,000 Hz - -AI prompt button messes up the thumb button harmony Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Razer has been updating its gaming mouse lineup systematically over the past two years, and it's finally the Basilisk's turn to get a real update. The last update we saw to the Basilisk line was the Basilisk V3 Pro 35K in October 2024, which was basically just the Basilisk V3 Pro with a new sensor. The Basilisk isn't Razer's most popular gaming mouse line, but it is the more versatile, all-rounder line for people who aren't chasing performance above all else. The Basilisk V4 Pro maintains the general design of its predecessor — a contoured, right-handed gaming mouse with bright RGB lighting and a handful of extra buttons, for the serious gamer who isn't trying to break esports records. It features Razer's newest Focus Pro 50K optical sensor, gen-4 optical mouse switches, and up to an 8,000 Hz polling rate, plus multiple forms of connectivity and up to 200 hours of battery life (over 2.4GHz at 1,000 Hz). It is admittedly pricey, like all of Razer's flagship mice, at $169.99 for both colorways (black and white), and it launched with Razer's Mouse Dock V2 Pro — which is sold separately for $69.99. Design and Comfort of the Basilisk V4 Pro Following in the footsteps of its other recent next-gen mouse launches, Razer has kept the design of the Basilisk V4 Pro largely the same. The Basilisk V4 Pro has basically the same size and shape as its predecessor — it has a right-handed ergonomic shape with a contoured thumb rest and a hump that sits slightly back and to the left. It has large primary mouse buttons with shallow finger grooves, and a slight contour on its outer edge that makes it relatively easy to pick up and move. It's not exactly the same as the V3 Pro, however. The V4 Pro has two new buttons, for a total of 12 programmable buttons on the mouse: the left and right primary buttons, three thumb buttons (instead of the usual two) and a trigger button in the thumb groove, a clickable tilt wheel (three "buttons" — center click and left/right click), two buttons above the tilt wheel, and an extra button on the left side of the left mouse button. The third thumb button and the extra button on the left mouse button are the new ones; the third thumb button sits in front of the first two and is set to open up Razer's AI prompt by default, while the extra button on the left mouse button is set to switch through profiles by default. I'm... actually not a big fan of the new buttons. Or, well, I don't really think they're necessary — the Basilisk already had plenty of buttons for a mouse that's not all about having buttons, and I don't really see myself incorporating these new buttons into my workflow in the near future. The extra button on the left mouse button is a little too far forward — this is a very long mouse (it measures 5.02 inches / 127.5mm long), and the extra button is right at the front edge. I have medium-sized hands and relatively long fingers, and the button felt too far for me to press comfortably. It's not a big deal if you plan to leave it set as a profile switch button (which are often located on the bottom of mice), but it's not really viable as a real extra button. Worse, however, is the location of the third thumb button — the AI prompt button — which is located in line with the other two thumb buttons. I generally have no issue with three rows of thumb buttons, as my daily driver is the Razer Naga V3 Pro, but this new AI button is the same size as the other thumb buttons and it pushes everything back a little. This puts the first thumb button (MB4) back too far to press comfortably (and that's a mouse button I use often). And while you can swap the buttons around, the AI prompt button is slightly too far forward. Basically, there are now three buttons where there should be only two, and they all feel slightly off. The tilt wheel has three different modes you can switch through with the button right above it: two tactile modes (24 and 48 steps), and free-spin mode. I generally love free-spin mode, but the tilt wheel on the Basilisk V4 Pro is a little too sensitive and will backscroll if you even think about moving your finger near it. The precision-tactile scroll hits a great balance and feels great, however, so this didn't bother me too much. The Basilisk V4 Pro comes in both black and white colorways; ours came in white, which has shiny black accents so it's a little more Stormtrooper than iPod. It has a smooth matte white body with dimpled rubber texturing for grip on both sides. While it's nice to have built-in side grips, I suspect they will wear down like the grips on the V3 Pro — and then you'll have to find or make your own grip tape, as the mouse comes with none. The mouse is roughly the same size as its predecessor, but it weighs less: the black version weighs 3.53 ounces (100g), which is almost half an ounce lighter than the V3 Pro 35K (3.95oz / 112g). It's not an ultralightweight mouse (or anywhere close), but the weight difference is noticeable and the mouse is definitely easier to pick up. On the bottom of the mouse, you'll find pure PTFE feet — two near the front, a strip at the back, and a strip under the thumbrest, as well as a strip around the sensor, a power switch, and a connection switch button that is not programmable. In the box, the Basilisk V4 Pro comes with a USB-A dongle, a USB-A to USB-C converter, and a 6-foot (2m) braided USB-C to USB-A cable. While the cable is braided, it is not one of Razer's flexible HyperFlex cables — it's meant for charging the mouse and plugging the dongle into your PC, not for using the mouse in its wired form. The Basilisk V4 Pro sports Razer's latest optical sensor, which is the Focus Pro 50K Gen-3 optical sensor. It has a maximum resolution of 50,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 930 IPS, and it can handle up to 90 G's of force. This is the third Razer mouse to feature this sensor (others are the Viper V4 Pro and the Naga V3 Pro), and it's a solid sensor that works with Razer's dynamic sensitivity (the sensitivity can be set up to change based on how quickly you move your hand) and rotation tool in Synapse. It tracks well across just about every surface, including glass that's at least 4mm thick. The Basilisk V4 Pro isn't an ultra-lightweight mouse, but its shape and grippiness mean it's pretty easy to pick up and move quickly if you're playing an FPS. The trigger button is right under your thumb, however, so you may accidentally trigger (haha) it if you have a tendency to pick up your mouse a lot. The Basilisk's shape isn't quite as natural-feeling as that of the DeathAdder V4 Pro, but it's a comfortable mouse for a variety of games — from multi-button-needing MMOs to competitive shooters (though, perhaps not for peak competition). While I still take issue with the placement of the new buttons, it is nice to have a few extra buttons without jumping straight to 19. The Basilisk V4 Pro sports Razer's Gen-4 optical mouse switches, which are rated for over 100 million clicks. The switches have a nice, crisp sound that's not too loud (not as loud as Logitech's, anyway), though it's not a mouse for those trying to minimize mouse clickiness. The primary buttons have a solid, tactile feel, and I had no issues with misclicks or double-clicks while I was testing. While the tilt wheel's free-spin mode was too sensitive for me to get to work properly, I love the precision tactile mode — it blends speed and tactility perfectly. Features and Software of the Basilisk V4 Pro The Basilisk V4 Pro is programmable with Razer Synapse 4 (not Razer's web-based version of Synapse). You can use Synapse to remap the mouse's 12 programmable buttons (14 programmable controls, if you include scroll up/down; the connection switch button on the bottom of the mouse is not programmable). Synapse has a variety of remap options, as well as a built-in macro recorder / editor. Synapse is also where you'll be able to customize the mouse further by tweaking things like the scroll wheel, DPI stages, and surface calibration. There's also a sensitivity matcher that will match the Basilisk V4 Pro's sensitivity to match that of your old mouse. You can also use Razer's Chroma Studio to customize the mouse's lighting and sync it with games and/or your other Razer peripherals. The Basilisk V4 Pro has seven RGB lighting zones: a five-zone underglow strip along the bottom curve of the mouse, as well as one in the scroll wheel and one in the logo on the palm rest. The lighting is bright and the underglow's five zones blend nicely — the underglow strip is tilted outward so it's pretty visible when the mouse is just sitting on your desk. Wireless Experience and Battery Life of the Basilisk V4 Pro The Basilisk V4 Pro has three forms of connectivity: 2.4GHz wireless, Bluetooth, and wired (via USB-C), though it doesn't really come with a mouse-ready USB-C cable. Razer rates it at 200 hours of battery life over a 2.4GHz wireless connection with a 1,000 Hz polling rate, which is excellent. This number does drop to 54 hours at an 8,000 Hz polling rate, which is... still pretty good, to be honest. The Basilisk V4 Pro launched alongside Razer's Mouse Dock V2 Pro, which is a wireless charging dock with built-in RGB lighting and an integrated 8,000 Hz wireless receiver. The Mouse Dock V2 Pro is sold separately for $70, and comes with a wireless charging puck that slots into the bottom of the mouse. It sits on your desk (it's small — 3.28 x 2.2 x 1.71 inches / 83.5 x 56 x 43.5mm) and serves as a magnetic dock and wireless receiver for your mouse. It has eight RGB lighting zones around the base, and it lights up to indicate battery level (flashes red when the battery is low). It's made for the Basilisk V4 Pro and V4 HyperSpeed, but it will also work with the Basilisk V3 Pro 35K, the Basilisk V3 Pro, the Cobra Pro, the Cobra HyperSpeed, the Naga V3 Pro, and the Naga V2 Pro (up to 8,000 Hz polling rate for all except the Naga V2 Pro). The Basilisk V4 Pro is also compatible with Razer's HyperFlux V2 charging mouse pad, but you'll need to connect to your PC via the mouse's dongle for 8,000 Hz polling. The Razer Basilisk V4 Pro is an expected update to the Basilisk V3 Pro / 35K. The bump in battery life, from 150 hours in the Basilisk V3 Pro 35K to 200 hours in the Basilisk V4 Pro, is very nice (and 54 hours with an 8,000 Hz polling rate isn't bad, either). While I didn't like the new buttons, I'm sure some people will (although I find it difficult to believe that every mouse and keyboard needs a dedicated AI prompt button), and the reduced weight feels good even if, at 100g, it's still nowhere near the ultra-lightweight category. The Basilisk V4 Pro is a great gaming mouse for gamers who want something a little more exciting and versatile than a DeathAdder V4 Pro, but not as button-heavy (or as heavy) as a Naga V3 Pro.

item.title: SALES: Which pet store loyalty program is best: Chewy+, Petco Perks or PetSmart Treats Rewards?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Which pet store loyalty program is best: Chewy+, Petco Perks or PetSmart Treats Rewards? At TPG, we're all about maximizing rewards on your everyday spending — purchases you would normally make anyway — since hotel points and airline miles aren't the only currencies worth earning. Chewy, Petco and PetSmart are some of the biggest names in the pet-supply business, and each one offers a rewards program to help pet parents earn cash back toward their next bag of dog food, kitty litter, hamster bedding, snake snacks... You get the idea. This guide will cover everything you need to know about the three programs, from how to earn and redeem points to elite status tiers and paid subscriptions, so you can decide which is best for you and your pet. Chewy+, Petco Perks and PetSmart Treats Rewards compared Chewy+ is the pay-to-play loyalty program of online pet supply giant Chewy. You can currently try it free for 30 days, after which it will cost $59 per year. This annual fee allows you to earn and burn rewards with Chewy as follows: - 5% back on dog and cat food (excluding veterinary diets) and all health and pharmacy items - 2% back on everything else you buy from Chewy. (Gift cards and pet insurance plans are excluded.) Rewards can be redeemed like cash toward a future purchase. You need only have $0.01 (10 points) in Chewy+ Rewards to start redeeming. Rewards expire at the end of the month, one year after they were earned. There is also a $100 annual rewards cap, after which you will no longer earn points for the rest of the year. Beyond the ability to earn and burn rewards, Chewy+ membership provides the following perks: - Free shipping on all orders with no minimum (there is a $49 minimum for nonmembers) - Exclusive deals and bonus rewards offers - A 24/7 pet poison help line ($99 value) - One free virtual vet visit per year ($50 value) plus 10% off future visits - Free trial-size samples from bestselling brands To see if it's worth it, let's do some quick math. To earn at least $59 per year in rewards and offset the annual fee, you would need to spend at least $1,180 on eligible food and health products or $2,950 on other products. Those are pretty high numbers to just break even. However, if the other perks present significant value to you — for instance, if you often place small orders that wouldn't qualify for free shipping or you don't have a 24-hour vet to call if your pet ingests something iffy — the membership could make more sense. And you'll get the most value from the program if most of your pet-related purchases fall in the health, pharmacy and non-prescription food categories. The program makes less sense for high spenders. If you spend more than $2,000 per year on cat or dog food and health items, or more than $5,000 on other purchases, you will hit the annual cap and stop earning rewards. Lastly, since many of the benefits are geared toward dogs and cats, other pet parents may not find Chewy+ worth the investment. With Petco Perks, all members earn 30 points per dollar spent on Petco brands and 10 points per dollar on other Petco purchases. Since each 1,000 points is worth $1 off a future purchase, that's equivalent to 3% or 1% cash back. You can decide how many of your points to redeem, but you must redeem a minimum of 5,000 points at a time. Points expire one year after you earn them. Other benefits include exclusive member pricing, autoship savings, personalized offers, a birthday treat for your pet and a free eighth grooming session. The only level other than basic membership, Premier, is more of a subscription than an elite status tier: It costs $24.99 per month or $239.99 per year. (This cost is per pet; you can save when you enroll multiple pets.) The costs and benefits of Premier vary by animal type, with options for dogs, cats, fish, small pets, reptiles and birds. Right now, new members can get an extra $10 in Petco Cash when enrolling their dog or cat or $5 for their small animal. For dog and cat owners, Premier membership unlocks additional perks like: - 15,000 points (worth $15) per month (expires 45 days after issuance) - 20% off every dog grooming or kitty litter purchase - Unlimited vet exams at Petco or 20,000 points ($20) toward up to two vet exams outside of Petco each year Premier membership isn't cheap, but it could make sense given your pet's needs, especially if you tend to refill your pet supplies monthly rather than stocking up a few times a year. Let's say your dog goes through a $30 small bag of kibble every month. With Premier, you could save $3 on every bag with the 10% food discount, plus $15 with the monthly 15,000-point bonus. That comes to $216 per year, covering roughly 90% of the membership fee if you pay annually. If you take advantage of other perks, like the unlimited Petco vet exams, the subscription could present even more value. PetSmart Treats Rewards is a loyalty program with three tiers: - Member (free to join) - Bestie (earned after $500 spent each year) - Very Important Pet Parent (earned after $1,000 spent each year) Here are the benefits you can expect at each level. Member: - Earn 10 points per dollar spent in stores and online, including services like grooming, boarding, daycare and training - Earn double points on PetSmart Charities donations at checkout - Personalized offers for savings or bonus points - Free shipping on eligible orders of $49 or more - 1,000 bonus points for completing your profile - The eleventh Doggie Day Camp session is free - Two annual Salon Reward Certificates with the purchase of a bath or groom Bestie ($500 annual spend): - One double-points purchase per year (you get to decide when to activate it) VIPP ($1,000 annual spend): You can redeem points for discounts on any product or pet service, or donate them to PetSmart Charities. Every 1,000 points gives you $2 off, so points are essentially worth 0.2 cents apiece. That represents a return ranging from 2% for basic members to 2.8% for VIPPs. However, you can earn far more points by taking advantage of the program's offers, which you can see in your Treats Rewards account. You must activate an offer by clicking the plus sign before you can use it. For instance, right now, I can earn 2,500 points (worth $5) on purchases of dog treats and chews of $25 or more, once a day for up to five days. Since pet supplies tend to be shelf-stable, I'll often take advantage of offers like these to stock up on my dogs' favorite snacks while earning extra rewards. You can choose when to redeem points and how many to redeem; just keep in mind that points expire 12 months after they are earned. Occasionally, some offers will grant you bonus points that expire sooner. Which pet store loyalty program is best? These three programs are easy to compare because their rewards are all redeemed the same way: At a flat rate in exchange for cash toward your next purchase. In terms of value per point, PetSmart beats Chewy and Petco with 0.2 cents apiece compared to 0.1 cents. However, the return you'll get depends on how much you spend per year and in what categories. PetSmart offers the best rates for all-around purchases (2% to 2.8% back depending on your status tier), but you can do considerably better at Chewy or Petco if you buy items in their bonus categories (up to 5% back at Chewy and 3% at Petco). If you spend a lot on dog or cat food and health items, it could be worth investing in a Chewy+ subscription. If you mostly buy store-brand items, consider Petco Perks. If your pet's tastes are more wide-ranging, consider PetSmart Treats Rewards, especially if you're willing to put in a little extra effort to capitalize on the bonus-point offers. As a longtime fan of PetSmart Treats, I love that I don't have to worry about a membership fee or spend time overthinking earning categories or caps. Plus, thanks to the program's relatively modest elite status spend thresholds (and my two voracious dogs), I usually have no trouble earning my way to extra benefits. How to stack credit card rewards with pet store rewards If pet supplies are a necessary part of your budget, you may as well maximize your rewards on them. That means not only joining your favorite store's loyalty program, but also making your purchase with one of the best credit cards for pet supplies. Don't forget to check your accounts for credit card deals like Chase Offers and Amex Offers, which can earn you cash back on your purchase as a statement credit. If shopping online (and sometimes in-store), you can also stack earnings through shopping portals. For instance, at the time of writing, Rakuten is offering 2% cash back or 2 points per dollar spent at PetSmart, Chewy and Petco. Here's an example of what stacking rewards could look like. A couple of months ago, I noticed Rakuten was offering 15% back or 15 points per dollar at PetSmart, so I decided to stock up on kibble, bones and more. I placed an order of $375, which not only ensured my dogs would be set for months to come, but also earned me: - 14,000 PetSmart Treats points (worth $28 toward a future purchase) thanks to my VIPP points earning boost and activating other offers, including one of my twice-annual VIPP double-points offers - 5,625 Amex Membership Rewards points (worth $112 toward travel by TPG's October 2026 valuations) through Rakuten - 750 Capital One miles (worth $14 toward travel by TPG's estimates) by paying with my Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card Now that's something to bark about. Pet costs can add up, but our furbabies are worth it — and pet store loyalty programs are an easy way to save. The great thing about Chewy+, Petco Perks and PetSmart Treats Rewards is that there's something for everyone, no matter what kind of animal you have or what brands or products you typically buy. Consider each program's earning structure and benefits, as well as your spending habits, before you decide which route to go.

item.title: REVIEW: iPhone Duo Size Comparison vs. 2026’s Best Android Foldables
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
The iPhone Duo is officially available today. Apple Stores around the world are packed, if today’s launch at the flagship Fifth Avenue location in New York City was an indication. If you can’t be bothered to rub elbows with customers with $2,000 to spend on the foldable, allow me to show you how Apple’s first foldable phone compares to the latest flagship Android-based models. First up, some reference for the iPhone Duo’s size. From left to right below, we have the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, the iPhone Duo, a U.S. passport, and a B6-sized notebook. As you can see, the iPhone Duo has the smallest footprint. What you can’t get in this photo is the thickness and weight. The iPhone Duo is about the thickness of three passports stacked together and feels substantially heavy in your hand. At 254g, it’s heavier than even the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Here’s the same comparison but with the outer displays turned on for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo. The displays on both devices are glossy and 120Hz. While the sizes are similar (5.5 inches on the Z Fold 8 and 5.4 inches on the iPhone Duo), the software is different. The Z Fold 8’s home screen works like a regular Android phone. Apple moved the dock from the bottom to the right side, which is also where menus and buttons are located for “Made for iPhone Duo” apps. Okay, now that we’ve got a sense of how large the iPhone Duo is compared to something familiar, here’s how it compares to not only the Z Fold 8 (second from the left) but also the Z Fold 8 Ultra (third), the original Google Pixel Fold (fourth), the latest Pixel 11 Pro Fold (fifth), and the original Microsoft Surface Duo (sixth): The iPhone Duo shares a similar D-shape to the two Pixel Folds and the Surface Duo. But Apple’s asymmetric outer display stands out compared to the rest. I have always felt the rounded left corners on the Pixel Folds looked strange. Above, the iPhone Duo, Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold open to their inner displays. The iPhone Duo’s nano-texture display really helps reduce the crease visibility and reflections. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has the most visible crease and the most reflective inner display. In the above side by side, you can, again, see how much less reflective the iPhone Duo’s inner display is thanks to the nano-texture layer. That layer is replaceable, but you should not peel it off yourself unless you want an ugly, wavy, and distorted folding screen. You can also see that the iPhone Duo’s inner display is shorter than the Z Fold 8’s. The iPhone Duo has a 1.4:1 inner display compared to the Z Fold 8’s 4:3 inner screen. What would a size comparison be without comparing the iPhone Duo to a regular bar-style iPhone? In the above photo, the iPhone Duo is next to the 6.3-inch iPhone 18 Pro (center) and the 6.9-inch iPhone 18 Pro Max (right). The iPhone Duo’s outer display provides 90% of the screen area of the iPhone 18 Pro. Moving on, here’s the iPhone Duo (center) with its inner screen open in portrait orientation compared to the iPhone 18 Pro Max (left) and an iPad mini (6th generation), which is also the same dimensions as the latest iPad mini (A17 Pro). Look at how much thinner the bezels around the iPhone Duo’s inner screen are. If the 8th gen iPad mini, expected to be announced at next week’s “Pray and Tell” event in Los Angeles, doesn’t have thinner bezels, I’m gonna be disappointed. And here’s how the iPhone Duo (middle) looks compared to the iPhone 18 Pro Max (top) and iPad mini in landscape orientation. Finally, here’s a comparison between the latest Samsung and Google foldable phones released this year. Below, the inner screens are open on all of the devices. I also threw in an unfolded passport and the iPad mini for good measure. Alright, now that you know the iPhone Duo’s size, are you going to buy Apple’s first foldable? Is the $2,000 still too much when a bar-style phone like the iPhone 18 Pro / 18 Pro Max does everything you want and has better cameras? Sound off in the comments!

item.title: SALES: 17 best private dining rooms in London: sumptuous hideouts for special occasions
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
The best private dining rooms in London are sumptuous enough to rival castle banqueting halls and gilded spaces in iconic hotels around the world. They’re blissful havens where, just for a while, the hustle and bustle of the capital’s streets become a distant memory, as we savour art gallery-worthy dishes among the people we love the most. Some are favoured by cash-splashing celebrities who shun cocktail bars for a soiree behind closed doors, while others make unforgettable destinations for milestone birthdays. Whatever you’re looking for, we’ve rounded up the prettiest of the bunch. JKS’ Ambassadors Clubhouse had the hottest tables in town when it opened its doors in 2024 and, judging by word on London’s streets, there are no signs of interest dying down. However, as couples feast on succulent chicken chops and pile tongue-tingling curries on plates in the main, jewellery-box dining spaces, larger groups opt to keep things more intimate in one of the several private dining rooms. The Jungli Room seats up to six, ideal for friendly reunions with a minimum spend starting at £400, while The Raja Rani Room offers space for 12 in a twinkling, candlelit setting. For summer soirees, there’s space for 40 seated or 60 standing on The Verandah. Address: Ambassadors Clubhouse, 25 Heddon Street, London W1B 4BH Private dining rooms often feel more suited for evening events – think plenty of dark wood, cosy corners and twinkling candlelight. The Italian Greyhound offers something a little bit different. Light and airy, this room is perfect for daytime events from long, giddy birthday lunches to celebratory events. There’s enough room to sit around 40 people, plus it has its own bar and terrace, so guests can spill outside in warmer weather. Food is traditional Italian – plates piled high with rigatoni and capaletti, crispy chicken Milanese and bubbling dishes of melanzane parmigiana – and there is an excellent wine list to boot. Those looking for a more laid-back option could book the semi-private area on the ground floor, perfectly positioned next to the bar but separate from the main dining area. Olivia Morelli You’ve probably heard of Dove. Jackson Boxer’s charming, buzzy Notting Hill bistro quickly found its way on to Londoners’ must-visit lists when it opened back in January 2025. What you might not know is that tucked beneath the restaurant is a seriously sexy dining den. Think low lighting, long tapered candles, dark wood and marble, with dusky fabric walls gathering at the ceiling to create a cosy, tented effect. We start with chunks of fresh focaccia, plates of pickles and Basque salami, before settling in for a feast. The main course is perfection – tender roast chicken with a silky Café de Paris butter, and platters piled high with salty fries. But the real star of the show is the shared burger course: plates of Boxer’s now-famous burger land on the table to be divided and devoured. The room seats 12, with a three-course shared menu starting at £60 per person and attentive staff on hand to make sure the drinks flow all evening. It’s a truly memorable spot to celebrate; for my 40th, surrounded by friends, it couldn’t have been more perfect! Sarah Allard Address: 31 Kensington Park Road, London W11 2EU Skye Gyngell’s award-winning restaurant deserves another accolade, for it’s home to one of the prettiest private dining rooms in London. Firstly, the location could hardly get any better – what better way to work up an appetite before a stroll through Covent Garden and into Somerset House, one of the capital’s most iconic attractions? Skye’s team create incredible waste-conscious dishes that reflect the seasons in dining spaces you’re more than happy to gawp up until plates land on tables. Choose a standing affair with canapés costing £12 for three or £18 for five per person, or take over a chic dining room for up to 36 guests. Address: Spring Restaurant, Lancaster Place, London WC2R 1LA Bob Bob Ricard’s ‘Press for Champagne’ buttons took social media by storm when the restaurant first opened its doors. It’s treaded the line between novelty restaurant and glitzy dining spot extraordinarily well, and the Soho site, in particular, remains a go-to for foodies as glamorous as they are ravenous. Best of all, the full à la carte menu is available in the 20-cover private dining room, removing the need to offer limited options in favour of a lacklustre set menu. Address: Bob Bob Ricard, 1 Upper James Street, London W1F 9DF Crisp martinis, oysters, steak and a graffiti-lined Shoreditch backstreet… one of last year's best, and most talked-about, restaurant openings, One Club Row, brings New York glamour to the cool and cobbled east London streets. While downstairs you'll find the restaurant's restored Victorian pub called the Knave of Clubs, head upstairs and you'll reach the private dining space called The Apartment. True to its name, it was the previous owner's (Les Trois Garcons) actual apartment known for some particularly raucous house parties. Now, the party returns for up to 50 seated guests who can dine on the much-hyped One Club Row menu which includes their signature pickled jalapeno gougères, classic steak tartare with beef dripping bread and of course – plenty of martinis and Manhattans. Tal Dekel Daks Address: One Club Row, 1 Club Row, London E1 6JX In addition to being one of London’s trendiest members’ clubs, this former brothel and home to Karl Marx makes an excellent base for an intimate party. The pleasingly green Marx Room accommodates up to 24 for communal dining and 32 across individual oval tables, while The Leoni Room, which bathes in natural light on blue-sky evenings, can host 12 for dining or up to 20 standing. Address: Quo Vadis, 26-29 Dean Street, London W1D 3LL Embark on an adventure of indulgent Japanese flavours in the heart of Knightsbridge at The Aubrey, one of London’s sleekest restaurants. Admire walls adorned with hundreds of pieces of art before smugly slipping into the private dining space fit for up to 18 guests or the private omakase bar for 10 seated or 24 standing. Feast on Izakaya dishes under shimmering chandeliers before shuffling into a connected private bar where some of the most skilled bartenders in town shake and stir their way into your heart. Address: The Aubrey, 66 Knightsbridge, London SW1X 7LA Mayfair’s most intriguing restaurant houses a host of secret dining rooms for various soirees. There’s the Venetian-style Italian Room and Bar featuring Italian Verde Alpi green marble and artwork by De Chirico, or The Swiss Room, with a gorgeous hand-crafted oak floor and colourful pops, for seated groups of up to 14. However, the private dining room atop many a Londoners’ bucket list is The Scottish Room, a spectacular space for up to 28 guests inspired by the history of the Highlands and sister property, the Fife Arms. Address: Mount St. Restaurant, First Floor, 41-43 Mount Street, London W1K 2RX It’s of little surprise that Clerkenwell’s bucket-list Italian restaurant houses one of the prettiest private dining rooms in London. Dedicated fans of the eatery’s Michelin-starred fare would prefer we gatekept this floral wonderland, but that’d be unfair. Round up a group of six to 20 foodies and devour dishes such as creamy tortellini, seafood sharing plates and, of course, Luca’s tiramisu. Address: Luca, 88 St John Street, London EC1M 4EH The circus elephants gazing down on Soho’s streets set the tone of this intriguingly fabulous hotel and its dining spaces. The eighth-floor dining room, seating 28 guests, has seen its fair share of spectacular parties and industry events in the property’s short life, with floral tablescapes illuminated by candlelight and, weather prompting, the fireplace’s glow. Address: Broadwick Soho, 20 Broadwick Street, London W1F 8TH Belvedere is one of London’s ‘if you know, you know’ spots. Those who are in the know are among the capital’s most glamorous foodies, and this resplendent restaurant has hosted countless glitzy events and celebrity soirees over the years. The Holland Park hideout is a strong contender for the prettiest restaurants in London, as anyone lucky enough to step inside can attest. Lello Favuzzi serves flavours inspired by his Sardinian hometown of Sassari, with seasonal flavours peppering impeccable pasta dishes and seafood delights. There’s Loggia, a private dining room for intimate groups of 10-20 overlooking the 19th-century ballroom, while the upstairs area is available for exclusive use, spilling onto a balcony that’ll have you dreaming of summer evenings in Verona. Address: Belvedere Restaurant, Holland Park, Abbotsbury Road, London W8 6LU We couldn’t recommend this West African restaurant enough, whether you’re dining beside the French doors as they’re pulled open on balmy evenings or heading upstairs for an intimate get-together. The intimate space seats a maximum of 14 guests, who listen to the clinking below as the talented kitchen team rustles up lip-smacking menus in the kitchens below. Signature dishes include BBQ prawn akara and Lagos chicken with citrus hot sauce. Address: Akara Restaurant, Arch 208, 18 Stoney Street, London SE1 9AD For a private dining room in London oozing character, look no further than this Grade II-listed, 18th-century pub in Fitzrovia. Expect classic pub grub executed extremely well, from generous portions of fish and chips to flat iron steaks followed by indulgent helpings of sticky toffee pudding. A dedicated space seats up to 20, but several areas are available for exclusive use, including the 30-cover dining room and the snug for 25 standing. Address: The George, 55 Great Portland Street, London W1W 7LQ Breads from the wood oven, meats from the charcoal grill… you might be thinking that Soho's Impala is a little bit like the other trendy restaurants taking over London right now. But you'd be very mistaken – not least because said charcoal grill is being tempered by huge feathered fans as they do in Japan. Chef Meedu Saad (of Kiln) has fired up an incredibly unique mashup of North African and Mediterranean flavours with a global spin, drawing from childhood summers in Egypt and growing up with the Cypriot kebab houses of north London's Green Lanes. The vibe is casual and cool. That's even more pronounced in the restaurant's private dining room that seats 8-14. Saad has written three menus, each with a choice of whole roast duck, wild seabass baked in bran, or cull yow chops with tail fat potatoes. Every menu opens with stacks of Impala's three wood fired breads and small plates for the table, followed by heaps of grilled sheftalia, beef short rib and sardines in vine leaves. Make sure you add a round of martinis for the table, served on ice. Tal Dekel Daks You’ll find a suitable space for your jamboree at Boundary, conveniently tucked just off Shoreditch High Street. The snug is a chic, warmly lit space for dinner parties of up to 16, while Below Boundary, with its double-height vaulted ceilings, open brickwork and marble floor, offers space for 100 seated or 150 standing. However, on a summer’s evening, there’s nothing quite like watching the capital’s skies turn a vivid shade of tangerine while surrounded by loved ones in The Orangery. Address: Boundary Shoreditch, 2-4 Boundary Street, London E2 7DD Mayfair’s chicest Italian restaurant is the perfect place for a private event, thanks to its townhouse-esque layout offering various interiors and atmospheres. The floor-to-ceiling bar is the ground floor’s centrepiece, making it perfect for cocktail parties. Upstairs, there’s enough space for 64 seated on the first floor, where the dining room spills into Sparrow’s indoor garden, while communal dining for up to 25 is possible on the second floor. Address: Sparrow Italia Mayfair, 1-3 Avery Row, London W1K 4AJ

item.title: SALES: Successful people are microdosing a powerful drug for glowing skin — and this founder is cashing in
item.description:
Source: Business Insider
In the dermatology world, Accutane has a reputation as the nuclear option for bad acne. It's the only drug that can shrink oil glands, potentially clearing pimples for good. But it comes with serious risks — primarily: a high rate of birth defects if you take it and become pregnant. Other side effects include sun sensitivity, high cholesterol, mood changes, and joint pain. Parents are scared to put their teens on it. Dermatologists often reserve it for stubborn acne, after other creams, cleansers, antibiotics, and pills have been exhausted. And strict pregnancy-prevention rules mean monthly check-ins, tests, and blood work. But in recent years, some of the stigma around the retinoid drug, generically called isotretinoin, has started to fade, as people have gravitated to a smaller, more strategic "Hollywood dose" of Accutane. By taking small amounts of the drug, maybe just a few days per week, many patients find they can maintain a dewy, glass-like complexion on camera while avoiding painful side effects like ultra dry skin, and the initial acne breakout purge that comes with heftier prescriptions. "I love the Accutane glow-up," Honeydew dermatology founder David Futoran, 29, said. For him, it includes hair that's less oily, and baby-soft cheeks. Futoran is partly responsible for turning Accutane from a maligned prescription of last resort into a buzzy internet sensation. He's found new ways to streamline and digitize paperwork, turning most of the required monthly doctor's office visits and testing for the drug into something people can do at home. Honeydew is now growing 3x year over year, Futoran said, and interest in low-dose prescriptions is increasing. Dermatologists are divided on the trend of microdosed Accutane. Yes, it is a very effective drug, and it can clear up most breakouts. But there are tradeoffs to taking an intermittent or low-dose approach, and some doctors say why bother dancing around side effects when you could get on and off the potent drug in months, and have clear skin for life? Futoran founded Honeydew in 2022 after spending years on various antibiotics and multi-step cleansing and cream routines, with his acne constantly coming back. His vision was to make prescription acne care faster and more accessible. He partnered with his longtime dermatologist, Dr. Joel Spitz, to build a telemedicine platform connecting patients with providers and treatments for acne, rosacea, eczema, and psoriasis. Yet Futoran was still hesitant to take Accutane himself, partly because of the logistical headaches. One morning, he said, he woke up with a large, painful cyst in the middle of his forehead. That was it, he said — he decided he was finally going on the low-dose form of Accutane his company had been prescribing. "I should have done that from the start," he said. "My skin is way less irritated than it ever was on any of the topicals, and I just have peace because I know it works." Accutane works because it shrinks oil glands by turning down sebum production. It triggers the death of some stem cells, which is great for clearing up overactive oil-producing glands, but very bad for developing fetuses. In addition to making regulatory compliance digital, Honeydew offers specially formulated lip balms, cleansers, antihistamines and supplements like Omega-3 designed to replace lost oil. Bringing a celebrity skin trick to the masses Celebrities including Chris Pine, Pete Davidson, Emma Stone, and Kendall Jenner have all been open about using this powerful oral retinoid to help clear up persistent acne. The shadow business of microdosing Accutane, though, using it as a glow up drug even for minor, isolated breakouts, happens more through a whisper system between doctors and patients. 26-year-old marketing manager and social media influencer Kennedy Faris started microdosing Accutane with Honeydew in the spring. About a decade ago, she watched her little brother suffer some of the rarer mental health side effects of Accutane, and she was worried about the possibility the drug could lead to depression. "My brother's a very happy person, so it was really scary," Faris told Business Insider. "I was really hesitant about starting." After struggling to get a prescription from an in-person dermatologist, Faris heard about Honeydew from a follower and partnered with the brand. She started on a low dose of 10 milligrams, working her way up to a standard 40 mg dose over the course of a few months. After years of trying different skincare products, antibiotics, and medications, she feels like she's finally found a more permanent solution to cystic acne. There are drawbacks to being on the drug, she said, including sensitivity to alcohol, sunlight, and some nightmares. But the real benefit has been her renewed confidence, optimism, and joy, with friends noticing she's "more bubbly and happy," she said. "I was like, 'wow, I was kind of depressed.'" Because the drug shrinks pores, Faris has also noticed her face and nose appear slimmer. "Everyone talks about the fake nose job," she said. Some patients recovering from real nose jobs even use the drug to lower surgery-related inflammation and shrink pores on the nose while their face heals. As testosterone therapy booms, more men are taking Accutane to deal with oilier skin. And increasingly, patients are lining up for low-dose Accutane for minor breakouts, just to be in the clear. People are gravitating to skin treatments that will give them the edge at work and on screen, Spitz said. "Everyone's on Zoom or Google Meets or they're on TikTok or they're on Insta, and they want to look good," he added. Some doctors worry that microdosing Accutane could lead to more health complications if people stay on the medication for years at a time. "In my practice, I just basically put people on the standard dose and then they're done at five months, and then they feel much better, Dr. Ariel Ostad, a dermatologist in Manhattan who is not affiliated with Honeydew, said. "Patients, once they go on it, their skin clears up really quickly, and they're happy, and they realize it's not as bad as they thought." A shorter treatment course means less time worrying about drug interactions, liver or heart health, pregnancy, sun sensitivity, or bone issues. Futoran said traditional dosing can be "absolutely the right answer for some patients," and roughly 40% of Honeydew prescriptions are at standard dosages. Still, he cites studies showing patient satisfaction is higher with low-dose Accutane, and said Honeydew patients on smaller dosages have "materially better retention." "The best clinical outcome is when patients complete their course, but faster is not always better," he said.
